speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can simply re-echo to a considerable degree the opinion expressed t,- hon' mwnber for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Kay), who acted as chairman of the select standing committee on immigration and colonization and presided over all its deliberations with great fairness and dignity, and in so doing I am sure secured the respect and esteem of all members of that committee on both sides of the house. Our deliberations were conducted in the most amicable manner, and upon the terms of the report as presented we are largely in agreement, indeed unanimous, I think, except with regard to one particular clause.
It^ seems to me that the matter of immigration into this country is one of the large and transcending questions upon which the public of Canada at present have their minds directed. There is not, I think, a great difference of opinion with regard to the necessity of developing our country by means of immigration into this country, especially from the British Isles. At the Imperial conference of 1921, at which Canada was represented by Mr. Meighen, the then Prime Minister, a resolution was adopted unanimously, as follows:
The conference having satisfied itself that the proposals embodied in the report of the conference on state-aided empire settlement are sound in principle, and that the several dominions are prepared, subject to parliamentary sanction and to the necessary financial arrangements being made, to cooperate effectively with the United Kingdom in the development of schemes based on these proposals, but adapted to the particular circumstances and conditions of each dominion.
At that same conference the prime ministers representing the various dominions of the commonwealth also set forth an unanimous expression of view, as follows:
2. The conference expresses the hope that the government of the United Kingdom will, at the earliest possible moment, secure the necessarv powers to enable it to carry out its part in any schemes of cooperation which may subsequently be agreed on, preferably in the form of an act

Immigration-Mr. Cahan
which will make it clear that the policy of cooperation now adopted is intended to be permanent.
3.	The conference recommends to the governments of the several dominions that they should consider how far their existing legislation on the subject of land settlement, soldier settlement, and immigration, may require any modification or expansion in order to secure effective cooperation, and should work out, for discussion with the government of the United Kingdom, such proposals as may appear to them most practicable and best suited to their interests and circumstances.
At a subsequent meeting of the Imperial conference in 1926, at which Canada was represented by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), a resolution was adopted approving of the resolution of the conference of 1921, the Prime Minister of Canada being present and approving of the previous resolution. First a special subcommittee report was presented, and then the report was considered and adopted by the conference on the 19th of November. The prime ministers of the dominions most closely concerned, Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, and New Zealand, expressed their appreciation of the advances which had been made in practical cooperation in respect of immigration since the conference of 1923, and emphasized the earnest desire of those dominions to aid further in the development of their respective countries with settlers from Great Britain up to the limit of their capacity. The report says:
As was pointed out at the previous conference, however, the rate at which the redistribution of population within the empire can take place must be governed by the rate at which the dominions can satisfactorily absorb new settlers; and it was generally recognized that a sound policy must be based upon scientific and carefully considered schemes designed to secure the settlement of suitable persons under conditions conducing both to their own well-being and to the prosperous development of the dominion in which they are established.
And then, after approving of the three-thousand-family scheme as having been a conspicuous success in Canada, the report proceeds :
With a view to providing inducements to settlers to remain on the land overseas the subcommittee recommended that facilities should be provided for assisting suitable settlers from Great Britain to acquire farms of their own.
Then finally a resolution was passed of which I shall read the last clause, as follows:
It (the conference) endorses the view expressed at that conference that the policy should be a permanent one. It recognizes that it would be impracticable, owing to financial, economic, and political considerations, to promote mass movements of population, but it is satisfied that, by continuous adherence to the
present policy, it should be possible steadily to increase the flow of population to those parts of the British commonwealth where it is most needed for development and general security, and where it will find the greatest opportunities.	,
That series of resolutions adopted in 1921, and reaffirmed and extended in 1926, proves to my mind conclusively that the representatives of this government and of the preceding government were quite unanimous in the view that it was absolutely necessary to have a clear understanding between the government of this dominion and the government of Great Britain with regard to a policy of immigration that would not only promote the transfer of immigrants to this country, but would secure for them employment on a satisfactory basis after they had arrived in this country.
With those reports in view I attended a majority of the meetings of the select committee on agriculture and colonization. But perhaps I was expecting too much under the circumstances. We dealt with the Immigration department in such a manner as to ascertain its workings in all their ramifications. We investigated certain rumours or suspicions which had been spread throughout the country as to the officials of the department being lacking in honesty, and another suspicion or rumour that members of the House of Commons had been trafficking in permits or letters of admission for immigrants from the continental countries of Europe.
At the outset I desire to say that after examining some of the witnesses and listening attentively to the examination of others from the department and outside, I came to the clear conclusion that whatever the department may lack in efficiency as it is at present constituted, there can be no reflection upon the honour or honesty of the officials who are administering that department. I also came to the conclusion that the suspicion created throughout the country with regard to members of parliament trafficking in permits or letters of admission to immigrants from the continental countries of Europe is entirely without foundation so far as any evidence was brought before the committee, and so far as I was able to ascertain by personal investigation of some rumours which were brought to my notice.
I deem it my duty to say that in the investigations which I personally conducted I think I found the real source of these rumours with regard to the payment of money by continental immigrants for their admission into Canada. Those immigrants do not under-
Immigration-Mr. Cahan

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Therefore we must look forward and adopt the best constructive policy adapted to bring about such a desirable result. I am convinced that the department as at present constituted cannot efficiently perform that great public service. Consequently it seemed to me and to some others that the government should now undertake the reorganization of the Department of Immigration and Colonization. Personally, 'at first I thought it might be reorganized on such broad lines as have been adopted in the Commonwealth of Australia, which recently established a development and migration commission for the direction and control of all schemes of settlement. One branch of that commission has the duty to make a complete economic survey of the industrial resources of the Australian Commonwealth, and I believe it has proved an important factor in the recent prosperous development of the Australian states. In this country I find that a number of members are not in favour of the commission method, although the commission would certainly always be under the supervision and direction of a responsible minister of the crown. Therefore I suggest a modified form in which that department might be created, having one branch in charge of immigration and a second branch in charge of the development of employment throughout the country in every form of industry. We cannot under present conditions bring large masses of immigrants into this country and set them afloat without providing here suitable remunerative employment for them. Under the present conditions and during the last few years we have lost by emigration nearly three-quarters of a million of Canadian youth whose places have been largely taken up by immigrants from Great Britain and the continent. We must provide employment in this country of a diversified remunerative character for the sons and daughters of Canada, and also such employment as will

Immigration-Mr. Cahan
enable us to increase our population by immigration from the old world, especially from Great Britain. .
We have at present in the Department of the Interior vast stores of knowledge with regard to our natural resources which are not sufficiently made known to Canadians and to the world. We have in our mines branch, in our geological survey and statistical departments vast stores of knowledge which are very essential to any board or body of men who may desire to undertake the industrial development of Canada. These stores of knowl-ledge should be rendered accessible, and further, full inquiry should be made by a branch of a reconstituted department responsible to parliament under the supervision of a minister of the crown; and that department should seek out and make known to the world all the vast possibilities of industrial development in this country.
I know that when I speak of industrial development in Canada there is always a suspicion that I am talking tariff protection. I regard tariff protection as an incident in the vast undertaking which I have in view and which I believe could be carried out by responsible men of large experience, hi^h intelligence and executive training and ability.
I am not bringing forward this motion as a vote of want of confidence in the government.
I intend to ask that certain matters which I shall bring to the attention of the house by resolution should be presented by the committee to the government with an earnest recommendation that the suggestions therein contained should receive the favourable consideration of the government, because I realize that so long as we have responsible government in this country we can secure the wellbeing of Canada, in the matter Of political administration, only by acting through the government which for the time' being occupy the seats of office. And however much we may desire to remove them at the earliest possible opportunity, we realize that until a general election they will sit stolid and content in the offices which they at present occupy and control.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that I can better present my views than by reading the resolution which I am about to propose, because I do not now intend to consume even the forty minutes at my disposal. I move, seconded by Mr. Arthurs:
That the said report be not now concurred in. but that it be recommitted to the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization with instructions that they have power to amend the same and to recommend that the
following suggestions and recommendations receive the favourable consideration of the government, viz:
1.	The evidence taken by the committee and the reasonable implications of such evidence disclose that in the matter of immigration into Canada, particularly from Great Britain and Northern Ireland, no effective measures are now being taken to secure the active and efficient cooperation, with the Department of Colonization and Immigration, of the Colonization departments of the Canadian National Railways and of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and of the various other organizations, associations and agencies which are engaged in the work of immigration, colonization and settlement in Canada.
2.	It is evident that the Department of Immigration and Colonization as at present constituted and administered is incompetent to procure the effective coordination and cooperation of all these various organizations in the work of immigration, colonization and land settlement.
3.	The matter of immigration into Canada is of mutual concern to Great Britain, with its congestion of population and prevalent unemployment, and to Canada with its widely extended territory and its sparse population; but neither country may be well served by the mere transport to Canada annually of large numbers of people who are left to make their way in Canada as pioneers in a new country under conditions of life which to them are novel and difficult.
4.	On the other hand, the capacity of Canada for the absorption in large numbers of uew settlers is obviously limited by the existing economic conditions of this country and the possibilities for their speedy improvement. The cost and difficulty involved in the resettlement in Canada of our returned soldiers after the conclusion of the Great War, and their absorption into the economic life of this country, are indicative of the ramifications of the problem of procuring the migration of masses of people from Great Britain to Canada and their resettlement in this country under conditions which will ensure their future happiness and contentment.
5.	Immigration should be carried on contemporaneously not only with land settlement throughout Canada, but also with such development and extension of employment in Canadian agriculture, mining, forestry and manufacturing as will rapidly absorb incoming settlers. Such immigration and land settlement on an extensive scale will eventually require not only large appropriations from the federal treasury for the direction, control and maintenance of such a comprehensive national undertaking, but it will also involve the establishment throughout Canada by private enterprise and by the investment of private capital of such profitable and diversified industries of all kinds as are suitable to our climatic and economic conditions.
6.	The key to the solution of the whole problem of immigration to Canada is the provision of adequate employment, in all branches of domestic industry in Canada, not only for our Canadian people, but also for the large numbers of immigrants from other countries who may be induced to settle in Canada.
7.	If existing economic conditions are more or less completely ignored and opportunities for
Immigration-Mr. Cahan

employment are not widely extended, large migrations of people to this country will inevitably result in increasing the problems of domestic unemployment in Canada, especially in the winter season, and in lowering the standards of life which are at present enjoyed by those resident in Canada who are now engaged in industrial pursuits; both of which tendencies will, in turn, seriously react adversely upon the flow of immigration into Canada.
8.	The committee, therefore, recommend that a department of Immigration, Colonization and Industrial Development be organized forthwith, which shall be under the administration of a responsible minister of the crown and which shall consist of two branches, each under the direction of a superintendent of intellectual strength and considerable business experience.
9.	The duty of the immigration and colonization branch of the said proposed department should be;
(a)	To procure the cooperation of the several provincial governments with the work of said proposed department;
(b)	To coordinate the work of all organizations, associations and agencies, which are now engaged in promoting immigration into Canada, under one supreme direction and control, for the more efficient carrying out of the undertakings which all have in common;
(c)	To ensure, in so far as practicable, that a majority of the settlers emigrating from other countries to Canada shall be such as may be physically and mentally adapted to the conditions of life in this northern country and likely to be readily assimilated by our existing population;
(d)	To make adequate financial provision for the settlement upon the vacant lands throughout Canada, which are suitable for agriculture, of families who appear, with reasonable certainty, to be adapted for agricultural pursuits;
(e)	To provide facilities for the settlement in the more recently organized provinces of Canada of settlers from the older provinces, who, as were thousands of the earlier settlers in the west, are intent upon leaving their homes in the east in search of wider opportunities for self-improvement in the new agricultural and mining districts which are now, from time to time, being opened up for settlement and development in the west; and
{f) To direct, supervise and control all schemes of settlement in the more sparsely settled districts of Canada.
10.	The duty of the industrial development branch of said proposed department should be:
_ (a) To act in close cooperation with the immigration and colonization branch:
(b)	To make a complete economic survey and study of the industrial resources of Canada;
(c)	To advise in regard to the future economic development of the several provinces of Canada and of the Northwest Territories, with a view to the more rapid extension of industrial employment, and
(d)	To direct its attention particularly to the establishment of suitable industries in our smaller towns and villages not only in eastern Canada and British Columbia, but particularly in the three prairie provinces, whence a constantly increasing number of young men and young women, who have no special aptitude or liking for agricultural pursuits, will inevitably

emigrate from Canada to seek other industrial employment in the neighbouring republic, if similarly attractive opportunities are not afforded to them in Canada.
11.	The investigations of the industrial development branch should be comprehensive in character and be undertaken in a spirit of scientific detachment, in order that- it may receive adequate and non partisan political support throughout the whole country.
12.	And the committee are also of the opinion that the industrial development branch by a detailed survey of industrial conditions in Canada, would be able to recommend what new industries for the production in Canada of commodities, which are now imported in considerable quantities into Canada, could advantageously be created in Canada or be transplanted from other countries to Canada, without unduly increasing the prices for such commodities in our more limited markets, and so afford constantly increasing and remunerative employment within Canada for all classes of our population, and thus provide the strongest incentive to suitable settlers to make their permanent homes in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I submit this amendment not in any critical spirit, but I think in its wisdom this house should outline some constructive measures for recommendation to the government for their acceptance, such recommendations to be worked out by the government not perhaps in order to start a new era of prosperity but in order to accelerate the prosperity of Canada by ensuring employment in this country not only to our own population but also to ensure that those whom we induce to enter Canada will find remunerative employment here. Unless we concentrate our attention directly upon the necessity of increasing employment in this country it seems to me useless (to continue to bring large numbers of immigrants into the country and to disperse them from one end of Canada to the other without providing them with the means of earning a suitable living here.
PRIVILEGE-Mr. YOUNG (SASKATOON)

Because of my solicitations
to the Department of the Interior a move was made evidently to clear up the whole matter. This letter is dated Saskatoon, April 30, 1928, and I will ask hon. gentlemen to follow me while I read it, as it reveals what was done to cover up the tracks of the hon. member for Saskatoon in the mistake he first made in accusing this man of obtaining seed grain under false pretences. Mr. Tubb states:
I received yours at noon to-day. I waited for it because I was honoured by another visit from the gentleman whose card I enclose herewith.
Mr. R. B. Matheson, Edmonton.
He was accompanied by the subagent at Saskatoon, Mr. Collins. They came on Saturday, April 21, and stayed about an hour and a half. This time he, Mr. Matheson, said he was not asking for any money and h^d no authority to accept it, but instead tried hard, very hard indeed, to get a letter from me promising to pay $300.
Which according to the minister's own words he had no authority to do.
He showed me a letter from A. H. Hanson . who promised to pay $300 if the lien was removed from his land. I read the letter.
The subagent, Mr. Collins, followed my wife into the kitchen and tried hard to get her to say she was willing to sign the letter and told her the government could seize the property-
That is the cottage in town which they have struggled six years to pay for.
-and sell it if we did not pay up. My wife is now upset with her nerves over this; in fact, she is ill. I absolutely refused to have anything to do with it.
I hold in my hand an abstract of the title to this property. The date of registry is 1920. There is a seed grain lien placed against the property on the 3rd of July, 1915, five years before Mr. Tubb ever got this property.
I find in connection with the figures "1915," that the two figures that were in the place where the "15" is now have been erased, and "15" placed over it in another hand from that which has written the figures "19".	Mr. Tubb has written on the bottom of this paper:
The seed lien was put on two years after this mortgage was registered. The date is quite wrong.
I want the house to understand from what I am saying that this man does not owe this debt at all for seed grain. He had signed a quit claim to that property on the understanding that the owner was taking back the farm, knowing full well that the seed grain was against it, and the returned soldier was signing the quit claim on that condition. He went to the war, served his country there, and came back.
I have another letter dated 31/3/28. This was in answer to one I wrote regarding some correspondence:	To show how anxious they
were to cover up the tracks of the hon. gentleman, listen to this:
Last Thursday the Dominion lands agent from Prince Albert and the commissioner for the western district called on me. These gentlemen, after explaining that the amount of the lien was about $850, offered to accept one-half and assured me that the government would see that Hanson paid the balance. I refused to consider it, and after a lot of talk they finally told me that if I would give them a cheque for $300 right there they would at once have the attachment to the title removed.

Privilege-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
This was after the head commissioner from Edmonton had told me that he had no right or authority to receive any money whatsoever. If hon. gentlemen think I am wrong I will leave it to them to decide what was behind the whole thing. The letter continues:
They said they had authority from Ottawa for that.
I understand from Ottawa that they did not have that authority. He goes on:
. I absolutely refused to do anything, and they told me that if I did not make the payment within three days the government would take steps to enforce payment for the full amount. I learned the next day that one had gone back to Prince Albert and the other to Edmonton on the night train, and had not called upon Hanson at all.
Here is another letter that is relevant to the case:
Since I last wrote you I have had a visit from the subdivision agent at Saskatoon. He explained his visit was not official-
Not official, this time:
-but knowing I was somewhat deaf, he thought I had not frilly understood the importance of the interview with the commissioner. He said: "If you will take my advice, you will pay the $300 and save yourself a lot of trouble."
Then it was I went to the department here and offered my cheque for $300 if this returned soldier had to pay it:
I told him I fully understood the matter. I refused to discuss it any further.
I want the house to follow this a little further, to see how frantic they now became to clear the hon. gentleman. Listen to this:
To-day the 16th I received a long distance call on the 'phone from the Dominion lands' agent at Prince Albert. He wanted to know what I had intended to do about paying the $300. I told him I was taking no action in the matter. He said he rvould have to make a report to head office about it.
Evidently the report has not yet -been made. Here is another letter under date of May 23, containing a few more facts. I will read what is relevant to the discussion.

It is from the returned
soldier. He said:
You will remember I told you he (Dr. Young) accused me of fraudulently obtaining seed from the government and unknown to Mr. Hanson. This is untrue. Mr. Hanson knew the facts of the case as I asked him to finance me, and he refused. I had only signed the contract to buy the farm that fall (1914). Now the department is to try and find out what kind of a crop I harvested in 1914, and what became of the proceeds. This was the question put to me by Dr. Young. I told him it did not concern him or Hanson as I had not bought the farm then.

Not only that, but Hanson himself suggested to the returned soldier to go to the government and get seed grain. The letter continues:
As a matter of fact, I went to Hanson several times about the seed and each time he refused, so 1 told him plainly that unless I had seed I would have to move off his place and it was then, when he saw he was likely to have a vacant farm, that he suggested that I try to get seed grain from the government. He knew positively about the whole transaction and I, thank God, have a clear conscience, but to go back to a time prior to the signing of the contract does not seem to my way of thinking to have anything to do with either.
Another letter that is relevant to the question is dated 16/5/28 and to show you how desperate they were to clear the hon. gentleman of trying to obtain a sum of money, I ask the house to listen to this, and I want to say that this was never authorized by the department either:

This is purely a question of privilege and the point is whether the 56103-245
language used was parliamentary or not. If a charge is made against any hon. member as to his dealings with his constituents, that he has violated the amenities of parliament by doing something dishonourable which debars him from being a member of the house, the rule is well known. Such a charge is made on the responsibility of the member making it, who puts his seat in jeopardy. The case is then sent to the committee on privileges, which after considering it makes a report to the house. In the present instance the house is not called upon to decide who is right or who is wrong-the returned soldier, the registrar, the mortgagee or the member. The only question before the house resolves itself into this. In speaking last night in committee of the whole the hon. member for Rosetown used strong words against the hon. member for Saskatoon respecting a certain transaction-but before quoting those words let me say that the privilege of one member is the collective privilege of the House of Commons. To-day one member may be accused of dishonourable conduct, to-morrow another member. These are the words used by the hon. member for Rosetown against the hon. member for Saskatoon:
This is one of the most sordid tales of bulldozing and bullying on the part of a member of parliament using his official position as a member of parliament to secure the payment of a sum of money from a returned man which he did not owe.
That is a clear case of extortion. Such a charge made against a member of the bar would mean the loss of his gown, and he would be debarred from practising before the courts for a limited period of time and perhaps permanently. But that is only the professional side; he would also be liable to arraignment before the criminal courts, extortion being a criminal offence. This is the charge made by the hon. member for Rosetown clearly and openly in this house against the hon. member for Saskatoon. Further, the hon. member for Rosetown said:
I am here accusing the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) of doing this and trying to bluff this man into paying a sum of money which he was clear of for more than six years. _ I think it should be made plain that men in that position, returned soldiers who have since got clear of their debt, who had gone to the war and served their country overseas, should not be bulldozed when they come back into paying something that they do not owe. I have nothing more to say.
I declare that this is one of the most cruel charges that could be made in the House of Commons against a fellow-member.

Now, what is the rule in such cases. It is clearly set forth by Bourinot at page 304:
Prima facie, any question affecting a member is considered a case of privilege, but in order to entitle a member to bring it up on that ground he must show that it affects him since he became a member of the house and consequently in his character of a member.
The hon. gentleman concerned, in his character of a member was therefore right in bringing up the question of privilege a moment ago. I am bound to state that the words used by the hon. member for Rose-town are absolutely unparliamentary. I have been in the house for almost thirty-three years, and I must say that I never heard such a charge delivered by a member from his seat against a fellow-member. The charge is clear-as clear as it is cruel. Bourinot says that a member is not allowed to call another member a pharisee, a slanderer or a villain. He says that an hon. member must not say of another member that he has acted either basely or from base motives. Is not this tihe charge in the present instance? Is not the hon. member for Saskatoon accused of having acted basely and from base motives?-basely in that he extorted money, and from base motives, from the' fact that this transaction was carried out at the expense of a poor returned soldier, that the money was not used, and that the hon. member for Saskatoon-according to the hon. member for Rosetown-had no business to deal with the matter.
The hon. member for Rosetown is an old and respected member of this house, and I would ask him to be good enough to rise and accept the denial of the hon. member for Saskatoon. Moreover, I would ask him to accept that denial unreservedly. Bourinot states:
It has been formally ruled by speakers in the Canadian Commons that a statement by an hon. member respecting himself, and particularly within his own knowledge, must be accepted:	but	it	is not unparliamentarytemperately to criticize statements made by a member as being contrary to the facts. But no imputation	of	intentional	falsehood	is
permissible.
Acting under this rule I therefore ask the hon. member for Rosetown to accept unreservedly the denial made by the hon. member for Saskatoon respecting the above quoted charges which	he	made last	evening.	Ishould be sorry to have recourse to the powers that are conferred upon the Speaker in a situation such as this. I regret to say that this is the worst incident of the kind that has come before me as Speaker-the worst I have	known since I	have been	a
member of the House of Commons. I ac-

quit the hon. member of having acted intentionally in the matter, with a view to violating the rules of the house. Surely, however, he must yield to the rule which obliges him to accept, without any reservation, the denial of the hon. member for Saskatoon.

speechtext:
I rise to
second the motion of the hon. member for Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) for concurrence in the report of the committee on agriculture and colonization. That report as tabled sets out the conclusions arrived at after many sessions and after a great number of witnesses, twenty-nine in all, were heard. I think it is fair to say that most of the witnesses, while not entirely representative of all interests in Canada, yet certainly did represent a great many interests both varied and vital in every part of the Dominion; and the report as tabled reflects the opinions of the committee. Those opinions, summarily stated in a few Short paragraphs, are rather lengthy; they are mere statements of fact. May I now rather than later say that the deliberations of the committee were conducted in a manner which was a credit to this house. No acrimonious discussion took place on a subject which might well have been somewhat bitter.

Immigration-Mr. Glen

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
As I was saying, the deliberations of the committee were conducted in a way that must be a pleasing reflection to all of those who were privileged to be members of it. At no time did any hon. member conduct himself in a way other than for the benefit of the whole committee and with a regard for the seriousness of tihe subject under discussion. I believe every hon. member was seriously trying to contribute the best in him to the solution of what must necessarily be a long-drawn out and not easily soluble question. This same feeling which was evident in the interests of the work of the committee will, I think, also be reflected in the house in the present debate.
The reason for the inquiry was attributable to various causes. Some of them were trifling in character as compared with others, but I think the principal reason may be stated in two paragraphs: First, the widespread belief that we were discriminating against British immigration; and secondly, the loss sustained by emigration from our country to other countries and, in particular, to the United States. There were of course other causes, such as the alleged unrestricted flow of continental Europeans with which is allied the question of the activities of the steamship and railway companies. One other question which seemed to overshadow for a time all other matters brought before the committee was the issue of permits. I was glad indeed to hear the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) make the statement today from his seat that at the conclusion of the inquiry he was satisfied, as I think every hon. member was satisfied, that there was absolutely no truth in the suspicions that had been widespread throughout the Dominion.
I wish first to discuss the principal causes to which in my opinion all other matters will be found to be related and subsidiary. The first is that we discriminated against British immigration. Now from the report it will be noticed that despite the assistance given British immigrants, whatever be the cause, we are finding it extremely difficult to get from the British Isles the class of immigrants we desire, although it was stated in evidence that more money was spent by the depart-
56103-245i
ment in the United Kingdom than elsewhere, the proportion of money spent there being $16.67 per capita for each immigrant introduced into Canada, while on the continent it was 11 cents per capita. Mr. Maoalister of the Canadian Pacific Railway stated in answer to a question that they were spending in the United Kingdom twenty times-it might be as high as a hundred times-more than they spent on the continent. And Dr. Black of the Canadian National Railways corroborated that statement. It is true that only immigrants of the occupational class secured assistance; apart from boys and domestics it was restricted to agriculturists, save those who come under section 7 of PC. 183, which provides that an immigrant may be permitted to land in Canada whose labour or service is required here. And he must satisfy the minister. This is the clause which caused all the uproar and all the talk; it was said to deal with permits, but these properly should be called letters of admission. It must be borne in mii-nd by the house that there is a very limited number of prospective agriculturists in Great Britain; it was stated in evidence that only 5 per cent of the population of Great Britain are employed in agriculture. The British farmer and farm labourer to-day is in a much better position than ever has been the case formerly. He now has am eight hour day with a half-day off each week, and his wages are almost as good as those paid in Canada. You can easily see that the inducements we can hold out to agriculturists would not affect any large body of people, since in many respects conditions there are better than the conditions which obtain in Canada. As a matter of fact, purely along the lines of labour, .they have equal opportunities in Great Britain to those in Canada; of course I say nothing with regard to their prospects beyond the mere point of labour.
Now the question might arise, "How do you propose to people the Dominion of Canada with British immigrants in order to maintain its Anglo-Saxon character if you are not able to appeal to the agricultural class?" There are one or two answers to that question in the report, and with these I now propose to deal. I will refer later to the question of the domestic servants, but first I wish to discuss the major proposition of why assistance is not given to British immigrants other than agricultural labourers. Let me preface my remarks by stating that it does not seem to be generally understood that no Britisher who is physically and mentally fit is prevented from entering Canada at present; he is absolutely free to do so so long as he comes under the regulations which are now in
Immigration-Mr. Glen

effect. There are several reasons in my judgment why assistance should not be given to immigrants from the British Isles, and I think it was the consensus of opinion in the committee that to assist in bringing in a large number of immigrants other than agriculturists, such as artisans, clerks, and professional men, certainly would mean the displacement of a large body of Canadian labour employed here to-day, and it would certainly and inevitably reduce wages. When Mr. Dennis of the Canadian Pacific Railway was giving evidence I asked him several questions along this line, and his opinion was that the policy should be restricted largely to the encouragement of the immigration of agricultural labourers, and in that connection he made a most interesting statement which he claims to be able to prove; he said that each family of five placed in agricultural occupations justifies the employment of 1.73 men in industrial life. Another reason is that assisted immigration of this character would inevitably result in unemployment. At the same time Colonel Dennis stated that he did not believe any large number of the classes mentioned would be rapidly absorbed; the experience of the west to-day, even with assistance to agricultural labourers, only demonstrates that fact conclusively. There can be no indiscriminate dumping of large bodies of men in particular districts without resultant chaos and uncertainty of employment.
The outstanding fact which this inquiry brought to my notice was the paramount need for colonization rather than for immigration. It is recommended in the report that efforts should be made to reduce steamship rates, which reduction when effected will mean the abolition of any assistance to any immigrants other than youths or domestic servants. It might be said that this would result in the indiscriminate dumping into Canada of large bodies of those people whom Colonel Dennis stated could not be rapidly absorbed, but the answer is that that result does not accord with experience. It has been stated in this house even during this session that large numbers of men are migrating to the United States to seek employment. It is an undoubted fact that for several years past the United States have been in the position of being able to absorb a large number of men, and men are just like capital; they seek their best market, and naturally they went to the United States. However, the converse is also true; at present one does not hear the tales about Canada that we used to hear. There has been created in Canada an atmosphere, psychological if you like, that we are on the

eve of a tremendous industrial development; whether or not that be true it is a fact that we are bringing back from the United States men who went there years ago; they are now seeking employment in Canada. The fact is that labour will only seek the place where it may be utilized; if we have employment in Canada men will come here, and the indiscriminate dumping which might be expected through the lowering of the steamship rates will not take place because I am quite sure that no man is likely to come to Canada from the old country without making sure of an opportunity to obtain employment here.
I am not afraid that when passages are reduced to what they were before the war, even if we have a large influx of men and women into this country, we will create any change in the unemployment conditions which have been created under our present system. It seems to me that with this arrangement the question of immigration will resolve itself into a question as to what restrictions are to be imposed against Britishers.
I would like to remind the house that in connection with the immigration of youths the committee have recommended that the ages be from 14 to 19 instead of from 14 to 17. If there was one particular scheme with which every member of the committee was in accord it was that every assistance should be given to youths and domestic servants. These matters are dealt with at length in the report and I do not propose to discuss them; the committee certainly were of the opinion that the age should be increased as I have stated. I realize that in the future there will be a much greater number of these youths coming into the country, and this might offset to a large extent the reduction in the number of agricultural labourers which may be caused through the abolition of the assistance granted. However, I would say that of all the schemes suggested those dealing with the immigration of youths are much more likely to attain the objects so keenly and ardently desired by the people of this country, among them being the retention of the predominant Anglo-Saxon character of Canada. The committee also recommend that the present arrangements with respect to domestic servants be continued. We can assimilate all the domestic servants we can get from the old country, nd I am informed that at no time was there any difficulty in placing them; the only difficulty was to get properly experienced servants.
Some evidence was given before the committee dealing with the large number of men in this country whose families still remain in the old country; one witness, speak-

Immigration-Mr. Glen
mg more particularly of Ontario, said there were 50,000 men whose families were still in Great Britain. At all events, it was felt that if assistance could be given to these men who have established themselves in this country and who are in a position to maintain their families, we as a government should re-unite those families, because most members of this house will realize that there can be no stability in the settlement of these men unless they are united with their families. After all, it is only the footloose who migrate and go to the states. Where you have a man with a family then I think you are likely to get a proper and suitable citizen. For that reason, the committee has recommended that assistance be given for the passage of families of men resident in this country who are in a position to maintain them when they arrive.
There has been a good deal of discussion with regard to land settlement schemes. Experience with these schemes in the past does not make one very hopeful. The soldier settlement scheme is the most recent, and I think this country will be fortunate if we do not lose a sum not less than fifty million dollars on that scheme. The three thousand family settlement scheme, while not the success it has been claimed to be is successful so far as one can appreciate at the present time, but it is still too early to discuss the entire success of that scheme. In this, as in all ventures of this character, you have to deal with so many variable quantities, particularly with human nature, which is the most variable of all.
In my opinion, the government would not be justified in embarking on those schemes unless and until the whole resources and activities of the provincial governments are allied with us. The justifiable complaint has been made by the provinces that we are indiscriminately dumping down large numbers of men in places whose power of absorption and placement is not sufficient to meet the problem. That is the keystone of the whole arch of immigration, and unless and until the governments come in and share with the federal government the question of colonization, I do not think we are ever likely to settle this country in the manner in which it should be. The federal government cannot shut the door absolutely on immigration, and no matter what may be proposed there will always be congestion in the larger centres. There will be surplus in some districts and shortage in others. It seems to me an inescapable conclusion that the provinces-I speak of the prairie provinces particularly, who are claiming there is no need for assisted passages, or no need for immigration-must
enter the field in conjunction with the federal authorities and carry on their share of the responsibility and colonization. This is not a new doctrine in the west, because we have agitated that the provinces should devolve some of the duties on the municipalities. The committee has recommended that an effort should be made to enlist the services, resources and activities of the provinces in this matter, and that the federal government shall contribute a large part of the expenses.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at three o'clock.

speechtext:
When the one o'clock recess
took place I was speaking of the question of provincial responsibility and I was saying that in my judgment the keystone of the whole arch of immigration depended upon cooperation with the provincial authorities. If there was anything revealed to the United States during the war, it was that there had been too great liberality in the admission of peoples of all races and kinds into that country. Millions of them were found to be physically unfit and millions of them also were found to be mentally unsuited to join the army. For this purpose, therefore, the committee has recommended that the government should endeavour to enlist the resources of the provincial authorities and contribute towards the cost of the machinery set up. Let me add that we have throughout the whole of this country large numbers of foreign-bom peoples. They have been invited by us to come to Canada and everyone who knows anything of them and who has had relations with them knows of innumerable instances where they not only have done well for themselves materially, but are proving and will continue to prove good citizens. The door is not barred to them by the present regulations and the committee have not entertained any thought of shutting the door. The same conditions apply now as formerly. Any European from the preferred countries is eligible for entry into Canada provided that he is sound mentally and physically and that he is in a position to maintain himself until employment is assured. Immigrants from non-preferred countries, namely, agricultural workers, domestic servants and those within a prescribed degree of relationship to residents legally admitted to Canada, are permitted to come here from those coutries and, with that, special exceptions may be made in cases in which the minister is satisfied that their labour
387S
Immigration-Mr. Glen

or service is required in Canada. Shortly, there is in the report nothing which prohibits or bars the door more closely against continental Europeans than is already the practice. The distinctive idea throughout the whole of the inquiry is that of offering inducements to the British immigrant.
Just a word in connection with the medical inspection in Great Britain. It was felt that the sudden introduction of the examination by Canadian doctors, the elimination entirely of the roster doctors, the blind spots which inevidently occur in most new schemes, the misunderstanding which usually arises through lack of knowledge and ignorance of motive, all contributed to the idea that the medical inspection was intended to restrict British immigration to Canada. It cannot be too clearly stated by the house as a solemn and serious fact that the Dominion invites and welcomes all British subjects who come within the regulations and has no thought of barring the door against any British subject who can qualify under the regulations governing admission to this country. The committee, in order to allay the misunderstanding that has arisen and to obviate delay and inconvenience, have suggested that local British doctors should be employed to make the examinations and that they should be paid by the government. They suggest that those doctors should form part of the Canadian organization and their examination be subject to the supervision of the Canadian medical authorities. I believe that provision will eliminate the principal objection to the present system and I do not think anyone can seriously object to Canadian medical authorities acting as the final authority from a medical point of view on all prospective immigrants.
The recommendations of the report speak for themselves, but there is one other matter to which I shall refer briefly. It is suggested that the assistance of the provinces should be invoked, but stress must be laid on the extreme importance which should be attached to the measure of support given by the railway and steamship companies and other organizations which devote themselves to this field of activity. The necessity of preventing overlapping and duplication of effort should not require to be mentioned at this period, but apparently it is necessary that it should be. All these agencies ought to be coordinated. I said at the beginning that this peace problem is greater than a war problem and' for those who speak of patriotism the best patriotism will be evidenced by the desire to co-

operate with the department in carrying out its work.
I was in hopes that the report would be adopted unanimously by the house. In the committee there were of course several differences of opinion on particular matters. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) had some objections regarding regulations with respect to homeseekers' rates and I presume he will speak to that in this debate, but I was of opinion that we came to the house with a fairly unanimous view that the report should be adopted. Therefore I was very sorry when the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) introduced his amendment this morning. I should like to say this with regard to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. During the whole course of the inquiry he was a most helpful member. I believe I am stating the opinion of all the members when I say that he adopted and maintained the standard which he set out at the very beginning of the inquiry, namely, that it should be on as high a level as possible and without any acrimonious debate in regard to peccadilloes of any individual who might come into the inquiry. During the whole of the inquiry the hon. member has maintained that high level. I might say, in passing, it was a privilege to work with him and to get to know him personally as I did. Therefore I was rather sorry that he introduced the amendment, for two reasons. With regard to the first part of his amendment which deals with the question of immigration, most, if not all of the provisions therein set forth by him, are contained in the report. He speaks in the amendment of the coordination of recruiting agencies; immigration from Britain to be regulated and provision for settlement; assimilation of immigrants from other countries; financial assistance and provision for settlers from the east going west, and direction and control of schemes of settlement in sparcely settled districts of Canada.
Most of these suggestions, Mr. Speaker, are embodied in the report. We have dealt with the 'teen age boys, domestic servants, measures to be taken for the reduction of fares, provision for homeseekers' rates, land settlement schemes and particularly provincial cooperation. While the hon. member was not entirely satisfied with the report of the committee, yet I thought that he was sufficiently satisfied with it that he could support it, and therefore I was rather sorry that he introduced an amendment.
With regard to the remaining part of his amendment, dealing with industrial develop-

Immigration-Mr. Arthurs
ment, it was suggested, and I think agreed to by the hon. member, that the last recommendation of the report dealing with the question of increasing employment, was to a large extent on the lines along which the hon. member wishes to proceed as indicated in his amendment. I might say that the last paragraph of the committee's report was introduced solely to meet the views expressed in the latter part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and I therefore was in hopes that having obtained that statement in the last part of the report, and being satisfied that the other portion of his amendment was already embodied in the report, the hon. member would make this a unanimous report. Not only was I personally anxious to see a unanimous report, but I did think that if this house could only give a lead to the country in the way of a unanimous report adopting the suggestions that have been made, giving a consolidation of thought upon the question of immigration throughout the country, we would be doing a very statesmanlike act, and if in the whirligig of time those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, should find themselves to your right, they themselves would have to administer the functions of government to which they had contributed their counsels.
Might I therefore in closing suggest to the hon. member, as I did in committee, that he forego his amendment? Now that he has made his statement to the house and it is on record, and this whole report will be spoken to by other members of the house, may I suggest to him, without seeming to be presumptuous, that if we could only send this report forth to the country as the unanimous opinion of this house, intended to regulate as far as we can the Department of Immigration, these closing days of the session will have been worth while. For that reason I suggest with all deference and respect to the hon. member that he should consider whether he will not, as he did in the committee, withdraw his amendment so that this report may go forward as the unanimous opinion of this house?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The question before the house at the present moment is probably the greatest question before the people of Canada. Thinking men all over this country are discussing the matter of immigration and of the retention of our population in Canada as they probably never have before. The country has been looking anxiously for the report which we now have before us, and I think I can safely say that it will be a great disappointment to those who have the interests of the country at heart.
This report in so far as it goes is all right, but it does not touch any of the essential points in connection with immigration. It is quite easy for us to agree on recommendations regarding, we will say, juvenile immigration. The committee were unanimous that the age limit should be extended to twenty years, as these young men coming to Canada were probably, and I think are now, the most desirable class we are getting into this country. It was equally easy for us to advise the continuance of the policy of assisted passages for domestic servants. There was no question about this at all; we simply all agreed to it. However, there were larger questions at stake. Matters were brought before the committee which are not touched upon in the report of the committee at all.
The proposition was put forward, and I think rightly so, that we should have a survey of all the provinces of Canada to see what opportunities there were for land settlement and for industrial and other employment in the various provinces; that this survey should be made continuous; that it should be made at least annually, and that men should be on the job looking after opportunities in each of the provinces of Canada. I think this is one of the most essential things that was brought before the committee. The appointment of the men in the different provinces I believe should be left to the province itself, but the Dominion government should pay the salaries of these men, the idea being that in that way we would have men more closely in touch with the various parts of Canada. The results of these provincial surveys would be exchanged between the various provinces annually, or more frequently, and could be publicly distributed. I think in that way thousands of our young men in various parts of Canada would be made acquainted with opportunities in another part of the country from the one in which they now live.
There is a peculiar situation in connection with our young farmers all over Canada. I say that advisedly because it has become a question in the west just as well as in the east. A few years ago a young man brought up on the farm, perhaps one of many sons, had opportunities close at home. There was vacant land near at hand probably, which he had the opportunity of taking up and supporting himself, and in other cases there were industrial opportunities in the small towns and villages nearby. But as these small towns grew ajnd th-eir industries developed, the farms were subdivided so that instead of having farms of two hundred acres supplying the needs of one family as previously the same area further subdivided supports half a dozen families but the farm of to-day
Immigration-Mr. Arthurs

with its reduced acreage can support only tile family which is on it at the present time. Unfortunately for us a great many of these industries in the small towns are not as progressive as they were in the past. We have many cases all over this country where there' are five or six young men growing up on the farm, and we know without being told-it is self-evident that unless industries are developed to provide employment for these young men, they have to leave the farm, and the result to-day is that many of our young men are drifting away from the farm and, unfortunately for us, to the country to the south. But if such a survey as I have suggested were carried out, and the opportunities in the different provinces were made known to these young men, I believe we would retain a great portion of our population which we are unfortunately losing at the present time.
I think also that the department should furnish to parliament at the opening of the session, or as early thereafter as possible, a statement by provinces showing the number of immigrants brought into each province for the preceding year, as well as the number of losses so far as that was ascertainable. Tins would give us something to go on.
As the previous speaker (Mr. Glen) has said, coordination is one of the great questions in connection with immigration. We have various agencies all endeavouring to bring immigrants to Canada. We have, for instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which, according to the testimony given before the committee, expended last year approximately $750,000 for immigration purposes. I presume our own railway, the Canadian National, will spend approximately the same amount. Then we have the various church organizations and the assistance in some cases of the provinces. For instance, I know that Ontario spends large sums on immigration agencies in Great Britain. But unfortunately at the present time there is no coordination. The two things we need are coordination and leadership; at the present time we have neither.
Your committee was also practically unanimous in another sense. Although it does not appear in the report, we were virtually unanimous in believing that the assisted passages should be done away with, outside of those already contracted for and the cases I have already mentioned-juveniles and domestic servants. We believe it would be much better to endeavour to reduoe the transportation rates generally in order to assist those from Great Britain who want to come to Canada on their own. There is a certain

class of people in Great Britain, as in this country, who are more or less independent; they do not want to come in as assisted immigrants, but to enter at their own expense and survey the opportunities here. We should make it as easy as possible for them to do this. In fact, we might go further: where a man came here and went on a farm, and proved to the satisfaction of the officers of the department that he was making good, his passage1 money should be returned to him.
We have had various schemes of immigration during the last few years, among them the three-thousand-family scheme. As the report shows, we were undecided as to the actual results of this scheme so far as we could judge from the report of the land settlement board. In that report it will be noticed that in 1925 we received 467 families, in 1926 we received 1,042, and in 1927, 1,122!-a total of 2,631 families. The great majority, probably the whole, of these on the average did not remain on the land more than a year. In spite of that fact there are already 261 losses, most of them absolute. Of these families, 92- have engaged in other than farm work, 45 have returned to Great Britain, the whereabouts of 27 is unknown-probably they have' drifted to the United States, 16 have been deported, 36 have purchased farms independently of the board, and 45 are employed on farms. I might point out that as regards these " losses ", as I term them, under this scheme all but 44 received assistance after arrival. So it is apparent that the loss is serious even under that scheme. Then we had another scheme put forward by the railways called the continental family scheme. Under this scheme 98 families ware brought to Canada. They were composed of various nationalities-Polish, 38; Hungarian, 17; Roumanian, 12; Jugoslav, 10; Lithuanian. 4: Czechoslovakian, 3; German, 3; Ukrainian, 3; Serbian, 2. Six families were of unknown origin-they themselves did not know where they had come from. Of these 98 families considerably more than half have disappeared entirely, 14 have purchased farms privately, 9 are in industrial employment, 7 are not definitely located, and the whereabouts of 26 is unknown. So this scheme was not very successful either. Then we had the Saddle Lake reserve scheme. The land was opened up for incoming immigrants, and they were supplied with horses, houses, bams, 40 acres of land broken, fencing, wells, and so on; all of these things were provided, and yet so far the scheme has not been very successful. We also had the Porcupine forest reserve scheme, where five hundred farms were set aside, ranging from 160 to 240 acres in extent.

3S81
Immigration-Mr. Dunning
This land was eventually thrown open to civilians. But I would point out that this fact was not broadcast throughout Canada. We have a large number of young men in eastern Canada who would have been glad to grasp an opportunity of this kind. It shows the absolute necessity of having a survey, the results of which should be available to all the provinces. Undoubtedly many thousands of our young men in eastern Canada would be veTy glad to have an opportunity such as was afforded to these people from outside. How many of our young men in Ontario, for example, crowded out of the home farm, would be glad to take up 160 or 240 acres of land equipped with horses, barns, houses and so on and be given 25 or 30 years in which to pay the purchase price without interest for the first year. It is only necessary to state the proposition to show how easy it could be worked out.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is one clause of the report with which I entirely agree. The reason I am seconding the amendment of my hon. friend from St. Lawrenoe-St. George (Mr. Caihan) is that he goes a little further along this lime and states his reasons more plainly than the reasons of the committee are set out in this report. I refer to the last clause:
Your committee would also recommend that the government make an intensive and comprehensive study of the possibilities of increasing industrial and agricultural development in Canada with a view to attracting capital and providing wider and increased opportunities for employment not only for our own people, but for prospective immigrants.
With this clause I have no fault to find except, as I said before, it does not go far enough to suit me. I believe we should build up our agricultural industry in every way possible. But in order to have a continuing prosperity and keep pace in population, we must also build up our industries. We must keep our young people in Canada by giving them opportunities, apd by all means those opportunities, financial and otherwise, which we afford to newcomers to this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not
desire to take much of the time of the house on this subject. I was not a member of the committee on agriculture and colonization, and having been busy with other committees during the session have not had the privilege of attending the sittings of this committee. I have, however, a peculiar interest in this matter because, as most members know, I was an immigrant to this country some twenty-five years ago, and any
observations I have to make are naturally coloured by my own experience. This country has treated me with wonderful kindness, and has given to me an opportunity greater, I believe, than I could have secured in any other country in the world-an opportunity, which, I believe, she offers to-day to any young man of the age I was-seventeen- who comes out from the old land. I believe the opportunities to-day for immigrants from the old land to Canada are just as great as, if not greater than they were twenty-five years ago when I came here as an immigrant. I wonder whether it is as hard for an immigrant to-day or an immigrant family as it was twenty-five years ago? I shall not offer any apologies for personal references, because the experience through which I passed, and through which members of my family passed, is an experience1 through which many other immigrants have passed and are passing to-day, successfully.
I came here a boy of seventeen and went out to the west to the end of steel at that time. I worked on a farm the first summer at $10 a month and was happy in so doing. I cannot express the great charm that the country had and still has for me; I cannot express the great charm that being entirely self-reliant had for me, of being removed from the congested conditions of the old land and translated into the freedom-freedom in the broadest sense-of the great west. The following year my father came; and by working together during that summer and the following winter at no high wages

wages never exceeding one dollar a day with board -we were able jointly to save enough money to bring to this country my mother and five sisters, all younger than myself. I do not cite this as an achievement because thousands have done the same thing; it was a question of the spirit behind, the recognition by those who were doing that sort of thing of the opportunities which this country afforded them and those of their families who would come after them. And it is being done today, Mr. Speaker, by the same kind of people as we in this house.
Conditions have changed very materially in this country and in the old land since that time. Our frontiers still exist; people are still going in as we went in twenty-five years ago; and there are to-day in many areas of the west, conditions almost exactly parallel with the conditions which I and others had to face at that time. There are differences of course; the radio and the telephone have made a very great difference and

Immigration-Mr. Dunning
so has the automobile. But men and women are still pioneering on the frontiers of this country with oxen just as we pioneered. And they are haippy in the process. I know of no finer spirit of neighourliness than existed then in those parts which we to-day call old settlements, then thirty miles or more from a railway, when nobody who lived there had any money to speak of but all were able to get along and were happy. There was a community life and spirit which it is not easy to find to-day in our larger centres and in our more wealthy communities. But not only in this country have conditions changed; they have changed in the old land. And it is because of that change in conditions in the old country that our problem with respect to immigration from Great Britain exists to-day, in my judgment, in very large measure. Twenty-five years ago, from the old land, British people emigrated to the United States, to Australia, to Canada and to New Zealand. The spirit of emigration was abroad in the old land; everyone was talking about the dominions. But in those days there was no old age pensions scheme in England; in those days there was no such thing as unemployment insurance. The degree of security which exists to-day for the old country man and woman did not exist twenty-five years ago; and the improvement in social conditions affecting particularly the poorer and lower middle classes

that element of security which has come about during the last twenty-five years-has undoubtedly tended to militate against a desire to emigrate and take a chance in a new land; -because, Mr. Speaker, it is quite a decision for a man to make, particularly a man with a family, to pull up stakes and move to a new land.
Now what do we find as a result of this change of conditions in the old land? We find that the British people, particularly since the war, have not been emigrating from that country to any other country in as large numbers as they did before the war. It came out, I believe, during the sittings of the committee that while Canada does not think she is getting sufficient British immigration she is nevertheless getting more British immigration at the present time, and has continuously through the years, than any other British dominion; and with the exception, I believe, of two years, she has received more British immigration during each of the last twenty-five years than has the United States, which is supposed to be the place to which everybody wants to go.
