speechtext:
I am speaking of the last twenty-tfive years. I looked into the figures recently and, if my memory serves me, only in two of the last twenty-five years did more British immigration go to the United States than came to Canada. And as the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) reminds me, even the quota from Great Britain to the United States was not filled last year. I mention these things to show that the problem is one rather of the 'lack of desire on the part of the British people to emigrate as compared with their former willingness and readiness in that regard1 during the period in which I came to this country .
What I have said raises of course two questions which are -bound to present themselves in a country such as ours, needing population to fill up our spaces and develop our resources: Shall we provide great inducements? Shall we try, by offering material inducements, to get those people to come to this country who are now more contented at home than they formerly were? Shall we try by that means to get more of them? That is the first question. And the second of equal importance, is this: Having regard to the nature of our institutions, to the kind of country Canada is, its relationship to the British Empire, shall we limit our immigration from other countries to keep within any stated proportion the immigration which we are successful in getting from Britain? I propose for a moment to discuss each of these questions.
With regard to the first; shall we offer further material inducements in order to get British people to come to Canada? Perhaps my experience ill fits me to advocate schemes of governmental paternalism in immigration. I am quite frankly of the opinion that it is not good for a man to come to this country asking: What will the government of the country do for me? If he comes in that spirit he is very likely not to be a successful immigrant. I make no apology for that statement. I have made it in the old land-and the -people of the old land do appreciate frankness and straightforwardness; they are naturally an independent people. During my last visit to the old country I was struck with the hundreds of people who asked me that question: What will the government do for us if we go to Canada? My answer was always the same: We offer you the same opportunity in our land as we have ourselves. You go there if you wish to help us to make that country, Canada, what we all should like it to be. Help us to build up a country in which you, -prospective immigrant, will have a share, a share which will mean more to

Immigration-Mr. Dunning
you and to those of your family who come after you than their future could possibly be in the land they are leaving. That was my answer invariably, and that is the view I hold now. By that I do not mean that we should offer nothing, that we should not display an interest in securing immigration to this country; not for a moment. We should put the facts before them. And I believe that the facts regarding Canada are quite sufficient without any gilding. The facts of the experiences of thousands of immigrants to this country not only from Great Britain but from other countries as well, are sufficient in themselves to indicate to any man or woman with self-reliance and ambition that this country is still the land of opportunity for men and women who will work and who will cooperate with those among whom they settle.
With regard to the question of employment, simple machinery is necessary to ensure that we do not receive into the country a surplus over and above those for whom work can be provided during a given period. There always has been a problem in Canada in that regard, a problem common to all countries in the northern hemisphere lying as far north as we do. In the nature of things many of our occupations are seasonal in character, and that operates to discourage immigration from countries where employment is more continuous than can be the case in Canada in our present state of development, at least in a number of our industries. However, that condition is gradually improving year by year. The necessary machinery already exists; since the institution of the Dominion-provincial employment service, operated co-operatively by the Dominion and the various provinces, it has become possible for each province to communicate its employment situation to the Dominion government not only in the aggregate but with regard to particular industries and occupations. I believe that we can approximate reasonable certainty with respect to opportunities of employment by the intelligent use of the Dominion-provincial employment service, in co-operation with the federal Department of Immigration. For instance, it is possible for the province of Saskatchewan to say, "We require for seeding, and in fact we require for the whole farming season, from spring until fall, so many -men this year." I will admit that in the west there is always this problem: When the crop is harvested and the grain threshed less men are required than are needed during the rush season. That is one of the problems we have to face, but
it is gradually changing character, although it will be many years before in winter agriculture it will be possible to take care of the number of men who can be successfully used during the summer season. I think every member of this house from western Canada knows that it is possible for a man coming to this country in the spring to get a job on the farm at good wages during the summer if he is possessed of reasonably good physique, intelligence and adaptability, and he can earn enough during the summer so that he can afford to work for low wages during the winter. There are men in this house who, like myself, have been willing to work on the farm during the winter months for their board, when the farmers did not have enough work to justify the payment of wages. I do not advocate such a course; I would prefer farming during the winter to be on such a basis that the farmers could afford to pay fair winter wages, and in many areas that condition is gradually coming about. So I believe that through the use of existing machinery it is possible to adjust immigration to the employment opportunities from time to time in this country.
Now with regard to the second alternative or idea which has been more or less discussed, as to whether we should limit our immigration from countries other than Great Britain because of the fact that our immigration from Great Britain is limiting itself due to the causes which I have discussed, I think I can say that I possess nearly all the prejudices of the average Britisher with regard to other races. I suppose no matter what race we spring from we have an inherent prejudice to the effect that our race is somehow superior to any other, and we may as well admit that none of us possesses that prejudice more strongly than those who spring from British stock. While admitting that, however, I have behind me some twenty-five years of close association with all the various peoples making up the population of the province of Saskatchewan and of western Canada generally, and with regard to them I want to say that in the main these people who have come to western Canada from countries other than Great Britain have become good Canadians and to-day, through the medium of our educational institutions and our school systems, are being assimilated very rapidly into our Canadian citizenshp, especially in the second and third generations. People came to our settlement from lands other than mine and I frankly confess that when they came there, with the insularity of mind which characterizes the average Britisher, I did not much
Immigration-Mr. Dunning

like them. But as I have come to know these people, to know their qualities and the contribution which they are capable of making, a contribution to some extent different from that made by the British immigrant, I have come to appreciate the fact that the Canadian of the future cannot be an Englishman; he cannot be a Scotchman; he cannot be an Irishman; he cannot be a Welshman; he cannot be a German; he cannot be a Ruth-enian and he cannot be a Ukrainian, but out of those different peoples it is possible to evolve, as I think we are now evolving, a type of Canadianism in the middle west which is true to Canada, which has a deep and abiding affection for the soil upon which it lives and which also is acquiring a deep and abiding respect for the institutions of this country, which are British institutions. Through the medium of Canadian citizenship they can be bound together in the empire. I am sure from my experience that it would be a mistake on the part of Canada to say that because we cannot get all the British immigration we may desire we should therefore limit immigration from countries whose population is of a type which experience has shown can be readily assimilated into our Canadian citizenship and can become good Canadian citizens if given an opportunity to do so.
I have just one other thought, and then I am done. The world has become considerably smaller since I came to this country; I mean that means of communication have become so much improved that now a man thinks no more of crossing the Atlantic than he formerly thought of travelling from the south of England to the north of Scotland. The time consumed in travel is much less than was formerly the case, and I am wondering whether it would not be good business, having regard to the attitude of mind of people at present, to base our immigration propaganda in the old land upon the idea of encouraging people to come and look us over in Canada rather than to ask them to pull up stakes and make a final move. That idea is illustrated to some extent by what occurred a few years ago, when we were at our wits' end to secure harvesters to take off the western crop. That yea? the Canadian Pacific Railway made an arrangement to bring harvesters from the old land at a comparatively low rate, but with an especially low rate privilege for the return trip on the production of evidence to show that the individual .had actually worked for a certain period in harvesting the western crop. My memory is that some 12,000 Britishers, entirely unselected and some of them quite unsuitable, as a proportion of immigrants are

bound to be and particularly when recruited so quickly, came on that Canadian Pacific Railway harvesters' excursion. I was making inquiries the other day, and it will1 surprise this house to learn that only about 2,500 of these people ever availed themselves of the low rate return privilege. Through that one experiment we secured more British immigrants in that year than we obtained from all other sources combined. That is what gives me the idea that if we could base our immigration psychology upon the idea of asking the Britisher to come and look us over, making it easy for him to get back if he so desires, we might achieve a greater success. In the past our whole transportation arrangement has been to make it easy for him to get here but very hard and very expensive to get back. Many of us during those heart searching early years would have gone back if there was any way to get there other than by walking. We know what homesickness means, and there may be the fear in the minds of some that if we make it easy for the immigrant to return home he may run away from us. The best answer to that is the experience which every returning Britisher has in the old land, and which I have had on more than one occasion. Literally hundreds of people who have been to Canada and have gone back home discouraged, come to us when we revisit the old land and want to know if there is any way they could be helped by advice or otherwise to get back to Canada again. We can rely upon the lure of this country, and the lure of the opportunities here to the immigrant, if he has once had the chance to get into his veins this virus, or whatever it is, which so binds people to this country and makes them want to come back to it once they have visioned its opportunities and associated with its people. I believe the idea is at least worth the experiment; instead of making it easy to get here and hard to get back, let us base our propaganda upon the theory of inviting the Britisher to come here and look us over. The world is a much smaller place to the Briton to-day than it was before the war; he does not look to-day on the crossing of the Atlantic as such a tremendous thing as he did before. It may well be that if we attempted to work along these lines we would reap a resultant benefit to our country.
These are just a few stray thoughts from one who has passed through the experience.

on the general subject of immigration, but before doing so I would like to refer to the statement made by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning). My own opinion

is that we stress the qualities of the British immigrant too much, particularly the English immigrant. I want my hon. friend to understand there is no personal inference in this.

speechtext:
I think the English
superiority of the Minister of Railways has been expressed perhaps unconsciously. We have not allowed people from other countries to make their contributions which would make Canada, not a little England or a little Great Britain, but Canada. We have imposed our thoughts and our culture on the newcomer and have stopped him from making the contribution he desires to make, and which he is capable of making. We put upon him a veneer of, I would like to say Canadianism, but it is scarcely that; but we are so anxious to convert him into a British subject that we prevent him from making the contribution to Canada which he otherwise would make.
For quite a number of years now we have made the error of cheapening Canada. We have been going out pleading and coaxing people to come to Canada, and by it we have cheapened our very excellent country. There is no better country in the whole wide world. When we make such an effort to induce people to come here and when we have such extreme difficulty in keeping them here once they do come, we do not send abroad the impression, which everyone of us has, that Canada is a fine country. We defeat our own ends by the very eagerness with which we go out fishing for people in other parts of the world. There are in this house men who have come as immigrants, from Great Britain and other parts of the world and who have made the very best of Canadian citizens, but they are not men who came here under assisted passages or were caught with a hook and line and special bait; they are the people who had the
initiative and the courage to come from their own country to this one. They have made a fine contribution to the welfare of Canada.
Personally I am in favour of just stopping state aided immigration. We do not need to grow so rapidly; great numbers is not a test of greatness. The overcrowded countries of Europe would be very glad to have our open spaces. We want to build Canada with a view to the future, and we should see that we are doing what is best for Canada and best for the people who come here, and which will show the best results in one or two hundred years. There is no real need all at once to fill up this country with people. If we treasure our own country, hold it high in our own estimation, and stop coaxing people to come here, strange as it may seem, we will get more people. In the country we hear it said that the farmer who wants the strawstack eaten builds a fence around it.
Our railroads want immigrants, but their object in wanting them is a purely selfish one. Most of us have selfish motives, but it is well for us, in talking immigration, to realize that the railways want more people in order that they may bring more business to them. The people who have land to sell want immigrants, because they want somebody on whom they can unload the land. It does not matter to them whether he sinks or swims-I suppose it does, really-but their first consideration is to get rid of the land and get the first payment, and then they are in a better position to get the other fellow when he comes along. The manufacturers want immigrants in order that they may have cheap labour. They want to be able to go out into the labour market and have less difficulty in getting people to work for them. The more industrial workers we bring into Canada the less chance there is of our workers getting a job, and the standards of living will be lowered. The business men want immigrants in order that they may sell their goods to the people who come in.
The agriculturists do not want agricultural immigrants, because if we bring immigrants into Canada in large numbc rs we will produce more stuff than we can {et rid of profitably. We would then be producing still more, and the standard of living would be lowered on the farm, and it is low enough now. Most of the farmers we bring to Canada are not class conscious, and farmers who are not class conscious are not good for this or any other country. We do not want farmers with a lower standard of living. We do not want farmers who are bowing and scraping to the manufacturers, to the banks, to the railways, and to the fellows who wear white collars and

Immigration-Miss Macphail
have soft hands. We want a farmer who is proud of his own industry and who will not let his brother farmer down. We do not want to lower the standard of living on farms; we want to raise it. That is the business of organized agriculture in Canada and I, as one of their representatives in the house, certainly am not in favour of dumping a whole lot of agriculturists into Canada who have no sense of the seriousness that comes from lowering the standard of living.
Some people say that we need more immigrants in order that we may produce more goods of all kinds. We have in Canada machinery and people enough to produce twice the quantity of goods we are now producing and we would produce them if we could get rid of them profitably. So on that score we do not need any more immigrants than we have at the present time. There is a disposition on the part of this government and of governments to bring agriculturists and domestic workers to Canada who, I suppose they think, are the two lowest on the social ladder. There is no inducement for domestic workers to come to Canada; there is no social standing in this country for a domestic worker. They have no unions; they have no way of protecting themselves. We should consider the interests of the immigrant as well as that of the person who wants to get labour conveniently and cheaply. I do not see any legitimate reason for saying to domestic workers in the old country that they will do better here than there. It is quite likely they are as hard to get there as here.
I am glad indeed we are doing something to stop child immigration. Children coming to Canada have been exploited. There has been an effort to bring them to this country in order that there might be cheap labour and cheap labour which could not make a protest on its own behalf. Had I been on the committee I should not have been in favour of bringing in more people between fourteen and nineteen years of age, because that is the age at which they can be most easily exploited, although it is better than bringing them in under that age. I took the trouble this year to read many reports on child immigration and the facts therein recorded would convince anybody who read them that children brought to Canada as immigrants have in the past been exploited. This is a system that should be stopped. They were not carefully examined as to their mental and physical fitness and our penitentiaries, jails, asylums and hospitals have far too 
high a percentage of people who came in here as child immigrants.
The time has come now when we should look on immigration sensibly, when we should take the view of the masses of the people on it and not the view of those who are spending a great, deal of money to endeavour to persuade the government to bring immigrants here for their selfish purposes. The people of Canada are not in favour of spending millions in bringing immigrants who cannot be settled in this country in a way that is comfortable to them or to Canada. We have in the winter time too much experience of unemployment, bread-lines, soup kitchens and other troubles in caring for these people to want to continue paying large sums of money to bring them here in increasing numbers.

Something can be said for them. It is characteristic of the English not to let the world disregard then-fine qualities. That is something which the hon. member for Southeast Gray should particularly appreciate. I know that in the past England has made many mistakes, but her record is written throughout the world, and she has done more than any other nation on the face of the globe to raise the standard of civilization to a higher level. Yes, there is something to be said for the English after all.
Now, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) stressed two points. First of all he asked: shall we try to get more British immigrants by offering material inducements? He rather deprecated this method. Well, the policy of the government has been along that line all the time that he has been a member of it, but this is the first occasion on which he has expressed himself as opposed to the policy. However, I am inclined to say to the hon. gentleman that the' government might offer inducements to get British or other people into this country, not so much by way of land, and so on, but by presenting for their consideration such a sane governmental policy as will assure them work in Canada. He referred to our having adopted what amounts to the quota system with respect to immigrants from the continent of Europe, and he rather opposed the idea. But it seems to me we have to ask ourselves this question: after all, is it worth while in our day and generation seriously to contemplate the maintenance of British ideals and institutions in this Dominion? If we answer that question in the affirmative, then it does seem to me that we must give consideration to the number of immigrants from those foreign countries that we can reasonably be expected to assimilate. I think everyone will agree that it will be easier for Canada to assimilate those classes of immigrants which we have been favouring rather than those from the non-preferred countries of Europe which we have been trying to a certain extent to exclude. After all, we must regard this as a fact, the movement of peoples from one country to another- migration is the word which will cover it-has in all ages had a tremendous influence in shaping the destinies of nations and their standards of civilization. That has been true of past movements, and it will be true for all time to come.
But it does seem to me we have made a mistake, perhaps not intentionally, in our past policy of immigration and colonization in

bringing in agricultural workers-those going on the land-assuming that there was no limit to our ability to absorb those who said they were willing to settle on the land. I submit this as a principle which we in this house should keep in mind in regard to immigration-we should aim to bring in immigrants of such a class and type that Canada's population would be fairly well balanced in terms of occupation and production. That should be our general aim. It has not been in the past. We have offered special inducements to those who signalized their willingness to settle on the land. What have been our principal sources of supply? The British Isles; continental Europe, divided into two classes, preferred and non-preferred countries; and the United States of America. The policy of the government has been to limit those coming from the non-preferred countries exclusively to people going on the land, agricultural workers. That has been our policy. The agreement with the railways, which we recommend should not be renewed in its present terms when the existing contract has expired, has been that they should bring out from the nonpreferred countries only those who were going on the land. How has that worked? We have brought to Canada in that way thousands and tens of thousands, every one of whom has signified his willingness or intention to go on the land. Have these people done so? I quote from page 735 of the evidence a short conversation between the minister and one or two members of the committee:
Hon. Mr. Forke:	The complaint we have is
that the newcomers are going onto the farms, but as soon as they have been here a year they do not go back to the farms, but into other employment.
Mr. Edwards:	They get into the country
under the plea of going on the farms, and then leave the land the next year?
Hon. Mr. Forke:	We may as well face it;
that is the idea.
Mr. Arthurs:	Does that apply generally to
these non-preferred countries?
Hon. Mr. Forke:	Oh, yes.
There is the situation. We have been bringing in thousands and tens of thousands of people from the non-preferred countries of Europe every one of whom got into the country on the understanding that he was to go on the land and remain there. But after being on the land a few months or a year these men leave and drift into the cities and towns; and they are the main factor in the unemployment situation in our cities and centres of population. That is what we are confronted with; it is one condition which in my judgment we ought to make every possible effort to put an end to. No one in this house will

Immigration-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
cast any reflections upon the ability of people coming from the non-preferred countries or from any country of Europe to become good citizens of Canada. No one wishes to suggest anything of that sort. We have too many evidences to the contrary in this country. But I repeat, notwithstanding that fact, that everyone will agree that there is more difficulty in assimilating these people than there is in assimilating people of British stock; and it seems to me we must have regard to that circumstance in certain parts of the country if we wish to maintain in their integrity British ideals and institutions.
There are in the report a great many points to which I should like to refer, but I will not take up my full time discussing them. With the report in general I am glad to agree. There is one clause of it with which I cannot agree and I so expressed myself in the committee. I think this was the only clause in the report to which I objected. I refer to the clause on page 8 under the head of Railway Rates for Canadian Landseekers. It reads:
The committee also recommends that measures be taken to ascertain whether the railways will restore the home seekers' rates in effect prior to the -war, making such rates effective east bound as well as west bound.
I object to that paragraph and I object also to a somewhat similar clause, though more extended, in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), namely, that we should provide facilities for settlement in the more recently organized provinces of Canada of settlers from other provinces who are intent upon leaving the east and going west in search of improved conditions and better opportunities. I object to this clause being incorporated in the report. Our committee was appointed as a committee on immigration and this is not an immigration matter; it is a matter which does not touch immigrants at all. It is a matter referring entirely to business within the country. It is an internal matter which has nothing to do with immigration. I object therefore to our considering it or expressing an opinion upon it. We might just as well have incorporated in our report a recommendation in regard to pensions or something of that kind, as to incorporate this. Moreover I object to the principle involved; I object to the government undertaking to make arrangements to move settlers from one province to another. The idea started in moving from east to west; but logically, if you assist in moving people from the eastern provinces to the west, how
56103-246*
can you refuse assistance to those in the west who desire to come east if they have changed their minds, believing that there are better opportunities for them in eastern Canada: Where will this sort of thing end? Transferring people from one province to another is not a function of the Immigration department, and I object strongly to the principle not only as indicated in the report but as stated in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. There are a good many things in the amendment with which I agree. I believe it is absolutely and fundamentally sound in pointing to this fact, that the key of the whole situation, so far as successful immigration is concerned, is in providing profitable employment for people whom we bring to the country. I believe 'that if this government will adopt a policy which will not drive farmers off the farms, which will not drive dairymen out of their business, which will not discourage-

Yes, this is politics; you cannot get away from the political side of it. I repeat what I have said: The key of the whole situation so far as successful immigration is concerned is to impress upon people in other lands that if they come here to farm they have a reasonable chance of success; that if they come to Canada to go into any other business they have a reasonable chance of succeeding in that business. And I have a right to ask consideration of this question: What encouragement is there to a man in another country to come to the Dominion of Canada and to go into the dairy business under present conditions, under the policy of the present government? What encouragement is there to a man in some other country to come here and go into the fruit and vegetable industry? What encouragement is there to people abroad to come to Canada and go into the sheep raising industry under the policy followed by this government? I say the policy of this government has not only closed factories in this country and deprived the people here of an opportunity of earning their living in Canada, but it has had the effect of reducing the reasonable profits of farmers and driving people out of business generally. How in the name of Heaven will you induce intelligent men in the old country to come to Canada under such conditions? Do you think you can stop their ears, their eyes and their understanding? If you invite them to come to the country to settle on the land the first question they will ask you is this, "Why don't your own boys stay on the land?" If you

Immigration-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
are honest you will have to tell them that the reason is that, due to the mistaken fiscal policy pursued by this government, there is no encouragement for the boys to stay on the land. That is the absolute answer. There you have the key to the situation. You have to provide a diversity of employment; you have to give an opportunity for people in various walks of life to earn a livelihood. How unfair it is, when you analyse it, for anyone to get up and say, "You must not bring industrial workers into the country because we have already all that we need of that class of workers, and if you bring in more you will lower the standard of living and lower wages. That would be unfair." And we are foolish enough, those who represent farming constituencies, to allow that to go unchallenged. Suppose you applied that reasoning to agriculture. There is an industry which every year produces far more than the requirements of the people of the country. We are looking throughout the world to find markets for our surplus farm products. Now, if that reasoning is good with regard to industrial workers, that you must not bring in any more, why not apply it to agriculture and say we are producing all the farm produce that we need, and we do not want more farmers? _ It seems to me that the argument would logically have to apply to the one as to the other. \ou must not bring bricklayers because we have enough bricklayers, says the bricklayers' union; you must not bring in any of this class or that class because we have a sufficient number to produce what these classes are producing. Bring in farmers, however, and every time you bring in five farmers you will provide employment for 1.73 people in industrial establishments. I think the whole thing is absolutely wrong and absolutely inconsistent. I repeat what I said a moment ago, that you must aim to bring in such classes of immigrants as we require in this country until you have a population fairly evenly balanced as between production and occupation. As far as I have been able to see there has been no attempt at all along that line.
The question of the feeling in the old country that British people were not wanted in Canada has been discussed in the house this afternoon. There may be a difference of opinion as to whether that feeling exists and as to whether there is any justification for it; many members would say it has no justification. I want to say just as emphatically that I believe there is ample justification for the belief which exists in the minds of many people in the British Isles that Canada does not want British immigrants. As a matter of fact the present government started

out wrong as soon as they took office in connection with this matter of immigration; they had! at that time as Deputy Minister of Immigration Doctor Black, president of Manitoba Agriculture college, secretary of the economic and development committee and a man of outstanding ability, recognized from one end of the country to the other as having studied this whole problem of immigration for years. His value will be realized when it is remembered that after the government dispensed with his services the Canadian National Railways placed him at the head of their immigration activities, which was a tribute to his worth. When the government took office they studiously ignored Doctor Black for a time until they forced him out- and appointed in his place the present deputy minister, Mr. W. J. Egan. Without making any reference to Mr. Egan's present abilities, because I think he has learned from experience and I am sure he would be the first to say so, I point to the fact that in my judgment the government did an unwise thing in dispensing with the services of a man who was so well grounded in this work and who had made a study of it during most of his life, and in putting in his place a man who, no matter what his natural capabilities might have been, was without previous experience. That is what the government did; that was their first mistake, and with all due deference I say they made a further mistake when they appointed the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization. He had had no vast experience in dealing with immigration matters; his previous experience had been gained on the floor of this house down in the southeast comer, where he was one of the chief critics of the other parties in the house; whether they went under the label of Grit or Tory, nothing was satisfactory to him. He was appointed to that position. I venture to say he has learned a lot since that time, but he had no special qualifications for the work, and the result was that as far as immigration was concerned it was regulated by orders in council instead of parliamentary enactments. One thing was tried for a while; then another was tried, and when they both failed something else was tried.

In my humble judgment, and I say it candidly and without wishing to reflect upon the present deputy minister, when the services of Doctor Black were dispensed with the logical man to assume the duties of deputy minister was Mr. Blair, who had been appointed by the Liberal party.
Now I would like to say just a word or two with further regard to this matter of discrimination. In my judgment the Salvation Army has been very directly discriminated against and very unjustly used. The Salvation Army started in their immigration work some twenty-three or twenty-four years ago; they have brought to this country over 100,000 immigrants, and they are able to say that less than one per cent of the immigrants they brought here have turned out failures. I would call that a good record, and I think everyone must agree with that. The Salvation Army established a big training farm in England and seven or eight other farms and centres in Canada; they have gone to great expense to carry on this work, but the government have seen fit to shut down on that work because they were obtaining from the boys they brought to this country a sum of money for the purpose of enabling the army to carry on their work and bring out other boys. The government made the mistake of
denouncing that principle; they said it was wrong, but that the government were wrong in their attitudte is shown by the fact that they have now endorsed exactly the same principle, although for a smaller amount. They have approved of that being done to the extent of $25, but they declared the principle wrong when they shut down on the work carried on by the Salvation Army.
There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer for a moment. In his evidence before the committee Dr. Amyot, Deputy Minister of Health, stated most emphatically that the Minister of Immigration had no right to override the decision of the medical officers in regard to allowing people to come into this country. Notwithstanding that fact, however, in looking over the proceedings of the committee-and this is where the discrimination comes in-at page 486 I find a girl described as follows:
Domestic work 3 months. Can cook, wash and do housework. Canadian government say: "She has been employed in mill past four years, therefore not eligible for the reduced passage fare."
I could name eight or ten cases of girls who are described as first class cooks and good housekeepers and who have had experience in that line of work for some years but who, just before they thought of coming to this country, were not engaged in domestic service. The Immigration department denied them the right to come out under this passage, and in every one of these cases the government merely said, "You can bring this girl out all right if you pay the money necessary for her regular passage." That strikes me as being rather harsh treatment and drawing the line pretty tight, if we want that class of immigrant in this country, and I think we are all agreed we do. I contrast that with the action of the minister in granting permits to remain in this country to persons who were deaf, blind or nearly blind, feebleminded; persons who were turned down by their own doctors as being unfit physically and mentally. I contrast the harsh attitude of the department in regard to this class of workers being brought out by the Salvation Army, and whose services are needed in this country, with the laxity of the Minister of Immigration in granting permits to those who were defective physically and mentally. The minister himself must bear a share of the responsibility for the claim made by the heads of some of our institutions in this country that a number of the inmates had been brought in, not only from the British Isles but from continental Europe,

The minister has to bear the blame for that. Again I contrast the minister's liberality in these cases with the attitude of the department in other cases. The minister can take up as many of these oases as he likes when he speaks on this question. The trouble arose, so far as the minister was concerned, in his not being able to cope with the situation in his department. He was led from pillar to post to do this and

Immigration-Mr. Jacobs
do that instead of managing the department.
I believe he will do better as he acquires more experience, like everybody else.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the key to the whole problem of immigration is to be able to show the intending immigrant that if he comes to Canada to go on the land he has a reasonable opportunity for success. We have to adopt a policy in this country which will stop our own boys from leaving the farms of Canada and going to the other side of the line. That means a complete change in policy. You can figure and theorize as much as you like about getting immigrants into this country, but what will tell in the long run and be the best advertising is the coming into Canada of men from the British Isles and from Europe who go on the land and write back home telling of how successful they have been in the different lines of endeavour. Such a man writes back home and says, " I have dome well at farming; I have done well in the poultry business; I have done well raising vegetables; I went into this and that and have dome well, and I would advise you to come here." No honest man can go to the people in the British Isles or on the continent and make the statement that there is a fair prospect of success in Canada under the policy that has been followed by this government. The whole tendency has been to discourage men from continuing in these lines of business. We have proof of that all over Canada, and you cannot get people to come in here and go on the land in the face of these facts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything in this debate and I would not have done so had it not been for the fact that I was a member of the committee that brought in this report. Inasmuch as I am not in agreement with some of the main features of it, I feel that it- is only doing a duty to myself to give some explanation as to my attitude on the questions submitted in this document. For the last ten or twelve years I have delivered in this chamber my annual immigration address. So far I have convinced no person but myself and it strikes me that ought to be a gentle hint to leave the work to more capable hands. Still, I belong to a somewhat persistent race' and I feel that perhaps as parliaments change, the seed may fall on fertile soil and I may be able to make at least one convert in the course of time.
The document which has been produced in the bouse to-day is noted rather for what it does not contain than for what it does. It was drawn up by a committee, the basis of
which consisted of members of the committee on agriculture, and consequently it has an agricultural tinge or flavour to it. One would imagine after reading the report that the whole of Canada consisted of agriculturists and none other. Might I point out that more than fifty per cent of the people of this country are not engaged in agricultural pursuits at all, and it seems to me that some mention ought to be made in the report with regard to those other people? The report is divided, as to the people who are to be permitted to come into this country, into three classes. This was already the rule. The committee are stating merely what already existed. There are three classes of people: first, the Children of light, the sons of the morning, the British race; second, those who are somewhat analogous to the British race, but not quite so. We might call them first cousins of the British race-the Germans. I can remember only a few years ago when to mention in this house the name of Germany in a sympathetic or Christian spirit-and I was the only one who did so-was to bring down on you the vials of the wrath of the ultra-patriots. The very mention of the name was anathema. We have moved since then and now the Germans are in the preferred class. Then we have the Norwegians, Swedes, Dames, Finns, Swiss, Dutch, Belgians and French. I can understand why France is included in the list, because French is an official language in this country. Thirty per cent of the people of Canada are French-speaking and it is the most natural thing in the world that the French are included in this class. But I ask myself; If the French did not occupy the position which they do to-day in this country, would France have been included in the list or not? I think the answer is self-evident.
There is another class, the lower or third class, the third stratum. They consist, not of cousins of the British but cousins of the German race. For instance, we have the Austrians. I do not know who drew up these classes, A, B and C, but I rather fancy that it was prepared in Washington where most of our rules of immigration come from. We have the Austrians in this third class, and I should like to ask those who are responsible for the preparation of this list, in what respect do the Austrians differ from the Germans? I do not know of any difference at all. There are no representatives of the Austrians in the bouse. Probably if there bad been their interests would have been looked after. Then we have in this third class, Hungary, Poland, Roumanda, Lithuania,
Immigration-Mr. Jacobs

Esthonia, Latvia, Bulgaria, Jugoslavia and Czechoslovakia. Russia, a country of 150,000,000 of people, is ignored altogether. They are evidently of such a class that it is not worth while even mentioning them. They are not on the list at all. Do you not think, sir, that among t'he 150,000,000 people in that great European country there might be some who would make good citizens of Canada? I would fancy so. There must be people there who are not satisfied with conditions as they exist in their country to-day, riven as it is by revolution and so on. Nevertheless they are not even mentioned in .the list. Are bon. members aware that 75 per cent of the people of Europe are debarred from coming to Canada by this class 3 list? Take for instance the countries of Norway, Sweden and Denmark in the preferred list. Why, the city of London and suburbs is larger in point of population than the whole of those countries combined. I say that not thirty per cent of the people of Europe are in the second class. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mir. Dunning) told us that the people of England do not- want to come to Canada because they are pretty well taken care of in their own country. They have the dole, the old age pension, unemployment insurance, and so on. How are we going to fill up our country with the proper people if the British race are so well taken care of that they do not want to come here? I would fancy that you would get them in places from which it is desirable for them to emigrate. People never emigrate from a country where they are satisfied. That has never been heard of, They go from countries where they are dissatisfied. The countries where the people are dissatisfied at the present moment are those which have gone through revolution and are just now in a topsy-turvy condition. I do not say that they are all dissatisfied, but there must be in those countries tens of thousands, yes, millions of people who would be very glad to come to Canada if they could find an opportunity to do so. But their names are not even mentioned in the lists. Yet we endeavour to proclaim to the world that Canada is open for immigration.

speechtext:
When those people leave
Russia, that country will not be able to see them for dust. They will not want to go back. My hion. friend is referring to the point that if they do not turn out well, they cannot be1 sent back. We have taken those chances in the past and I would be prepared to take some chances now.
The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) told us a few moments ago that we want the agricultural class in this country and nobody else, that it is useless for people to knock at our doors and seek entrance if they do not intend to go on the land. That was stated so pontifically by the hon. member that you would imagine it really was a fact, but if be had read the report, which I trust he has, he would see that people coming from Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Roumania, Switzerland, Holland, Belgium and France, are admitted freely to this country, no matter what their occupations may be. One hundred thousand painters can come in here from Germany, and you cannot say them nay, but if one painter from Austria, from Vienna, were to try to get in, it would necessitate my going with my hat in my hand to see the hon. minister and begging for favour for this Austrian. Is that right? Is that just? Why should there be a distinction made between these two peoples? They are the same class of people, identically the same; they profess the same religion; they belong to the Nordic race. In every respect they are first class, and yet this ridiculous distinction is being made. Then we have the cases of people from Poland, Germany, and so on, who are not permitted to come in. A few years ago Poland belonged to Russia, and Finland belonged to Russia, but to-day the Finns can come in, and the Poles not. What distinction is there between a Pole and a Finn? I challenge the minister to tell me how by looking at a Finn and a Pole he can tell which is which.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: The Pole may have fins.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
In that case the Pole might get in, but it would be his finish.

Immigration-Mr. Jacobs
That is the objection I take to this report, that you are making distinctions between peoples where no distinction should be made. I am not talking of Italians, Spaniards, Portuguese and people of that kind. They are not to be mentioned in the same breath with the British people; they are not to be brought into this country; they have no culture at all which thely can contribute to the development of this country; they are Italians, Spaniards and Portuguese, and although they may have had a history, their future is all in the past so far as Canada is concerned. They can do nothing for the upbuilding of this country; they belong to the Latin race, and all Latin races are rigidly excluded with the exception of the French, and a large portion of the French belong to the Norman race and can therefore be looked upon, by a stretch of the imagination, as Nordics. Is it not strange that in this country where we have nine millions of people, and could contain one hundred millions, we should make these distinctions between races as to whether they are Nordics or Latins. I say we are making a serious mistake in making these distinctions, and that this country is not in* a position just now to do anything of this kind.
My hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington, I understand, belongs to the medical profession. He knows that when he prescribes medicine for a patient he gives him two grains of this, three grains of that and four grains of the other, with plenty of water in it, and then it has to be shaken up well, and taken until relief is afforded. That is what we ought to do in this country in connection with immigration. We can take two per cent of this class, two per cent of that, and two per cent of the other, and they will all go to make up a people that we shall have very good reason to be proud of. After all, what is the British race but a conglomerate mixture? We all know that that is the case, and that there is no such thing as the pure British stock today, except perhaps in the fastnesses of Scotland, in the hills of Wales, or in the wilds of Ireland. It is only there that you find the ancient British race. All the others are a mixture of the Saxons, the Danes, the Normans, and people of that kind who* in turn invaded and captured the country. That is what has made the British people great; it is a mixture of all these races. Here we are in this country a population of hundreds of millions of Christmas trees and eight or nine million people, and we hope to make a great race by exclusion. It is an impossibility. The greatness of a nation is reckoned by the people who live in that country-not by its lakes and rivers and mountains, but by the people
themselves. Here we have a country which is losing to the United States hundreds of thousands of people every year. As was pointed out some time ago, within the last five years, 591,000 of our people have gone to the United States. Naturally they go there, because a magnet draws them. They have a quota law in the United States, and everybody from Europe except a paltry two per cent is excluded, although they used to take in from one and a half to two million Europeans annually. But they have been shut out, and where is the United States going to get people to (take their place? The United States is draining Canada dry of its people, and we *are sitting by and presuming to lay down by silly rules what classes of people shall be brought into this country to take1 their place.
I say that it is a serious mistake to select people on the basis of the country from which they come. A man is a human being, although he may be born in a stable. A Russian may be a very good man, and so may a Pole and a Ruthenian, even though bom in Russia, and a man may be a very bad and wicked man although born within sound of Bow Bells. You should select people for what they are worth in themselves. Look them over, and see if they can fit into the life of this country; to select them by countries, the method that has been followed in Canada for the last fifteen or twenty years, is a serious mistake. In the days of Sir Clifford Sifton we used to get from four to five hundred thousand immigrants a year *and they peopled this country. Whajt would this country have been without that vast body of immigration that caime to this country prior bo the last fifteen years? Things have changed. Our friends the farmers presume to sit in judgment upon the people who do not want to go upon the farms at all. I can understand that they want to have people go on the farms, but when it comes to selecting people for city life it seems to me that the people of the cities ought to have something to say about it. In this report practically nothing at all is said about immigrants except those who are to go on the farms, although fifty per cent of the people in this country are not on farms at all. You are providing that an artisan or anyone else may come in provided he comes from these particular countries that are mentioned in paragraph 6, but my objection to that is that if we are going to allow Germans, Swiss, Danes and Finns to come in-regardless, mark you, of the occupations
Immigration-Mr. Jacobs

which they are going to follow when they come here-why should we not extend the same privilege to Austrians, Hungarians, Poles, and so on? I am not here to make an eulogy upon the history of these races or to tell what the Hungarians, Poles and Austrians have contributed to the civilization of the world. Mind you, we are not asking to bring people in here who belong to a different colour; we are not asking that people be allowed in here who belong to a different religion; we are not asking that people be brought in if they differ in any respect from the people who happened to be born in Berlin or Hamburg. But I say that it is an outrage and a crime that we should have to come to the Department of Immigration every time we want to get a man admitted to this country from, say, Vienna, when a man who comes from Berlin or Hamburg is welcomed with open arms. The thing is an absurdity.
The report is void of common sense. Sixty men representing the wisdom of parliament held thirty-six meetings, and they have produced a mouse. I would be prepared to accept the amendment of my hon. friend from St. Laiwrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), but I think it is already incorporated in the last paragraph of the report which reads as follows:
Your committee would also recommend that the government make an intensive and comprehensive study of the possibilities of increasing industrial and agricultural development in Canada with a view to attracting capital and providing wider and increased opportunities for employment not only for our own people, but for the prospective immigrants.
That is the only constructive suggestion in the entire report. We spent our time in discussing whether we should widen the list of boy immigrants from fourteen to nineteen years of age, whether we should pay $11 per British immigrant, or $9.73, and matters of that kind. We have trifled with our time. We have not contributed anything to the most important question now before the country, and I think everyone of us who was on that committee ought to admit that the result of all our work is simply nil.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):

speechtext:
Immigration-Mr. Woodsworth
spring by transportation and other interests working in cooperation with federal government agencies in Europe:
And whereas no adequate provisions have been made by these parties for the supervision and settlement of these newcomers upon the land in accordance with the published intention of the government:
And whereas, because of this, many immigrants have been located in urban centres with nc prospect of sufficient employment to enable them to provide reserves for the coming winter and moreover thus aggravating the unemployment problem in such centres:
Therefore be it resolved that we place these facts before the Prime Minister of Canada, the Minister of Immigration, the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Labour, and the members for the several constituencies of this province with the request that immediate steps be taken:

(a)	For the placing of the financial responsibility for the care of such immigrants now and next winter upon the transportation companies and others directly responsible for the situation.
(b)	For the prevention of its recurrence in future years by the proper regulation and settlement of only such immigrants as the country can absorb.
(c)	The immediate planning of government works for the coming winter to give employment to our own citizens who are suffering from the dearth of employment and low wages caused by the recent influx of immigrants.
We all recognize that there is room for a certain number of immigrants in this country; but the point is that they are brought in without sufficient regard to the opportunities that are open at the particular time and with almost entire disregard of the seasonal nature of so much of the work in Canada. I had occasion a few weeks ago in the early spring to call the attention of the Minister of Immigration to the conditions which prevailed in my own city of Winnipeg. He rather made light of the situation. He said that he had heard from his officials there that these men would not take work. But the fact that we had discussed the matter on the floor of the house and the further fact that the men had held a parade in Winnipeg was sufficient to set machinery going so that, according to the Tribune of May 2, the officials of the employment service a few days afterwards stated that the week before work was found for 620 men, 234 going to farms, 229 to railway construction camps, 61 to highway costruction gangs, 14 to logging camps and the remainder to casual employment. I cite this example merely to illustrate this point:	A few days
before this the Minister of Immigration had told us that these men would not go to work on the land, and yet when the opportunity was offered them 234 went to work on the farms, the others later on finding employment in other spheres of activity.
The fact, is that we have seasonal unemployment in this country. Every year we have

to reckon with that situation, and it will be more or less permanent until such time as we make special efforts to provide for winter work. I think it is only fair to Canadians already here that the government itself should very seriously consider the advisability of bringing in immigrants in the springtime before there is work, substituting these immigrants for people already in employment here, and then later turning them loose in the autumn to forage for themselves, as best they can with the result that they finally land up in our cities, a charge' upon our urban authorities. I know we have discussed this question again and again, but the problem remains. It is only within the last few months that the government of my own province has issued a report on seasonal unemployment in Manitoba, It is only a few years ago since we had a conference of all the provincial authorities dealing with this question of seasonal unemployment, but we are content, it seems, to make reports and then allow the situation to drift along until something almost desperate happens.
With regard to British immigrants I think it is becoming increasingly clear that there is less disposition on the part of residents of Great Britain to leave their own land to risk the uncertainties of these newer countries. I noticed the other day a speech made before the manufacturers' association in session in the east. It corroborated the testimony which was given this year before the committee on industrial and international relations to the effect that, by reason of the provisions now existing in Great Britain for unemployment, for sickness, invalidity and old age a great many of the best workers in that country are unwilling to leave and come to a land where there are fewer provisions of this kind:. If we are to get the best class of English immigrants it seems that the surest way is to raise our social standards until they are somewhat comparable to those which now exist in England as well as in a number of countries in northern Europe.
The Minister of Railways made mention of the harvesters who came to this country and he rather rejoiced that so few of them had returned to the old land. Those who sat in the house several years ago may remember that a large contingent of those harvesters came to Ottawa, out of work, without food, and begging that something should be done in their case. And the most that could be done was to get a special car and bundle them back to Toronto. I am not so sure that that experiment ini bringing harvesters to this country was an unqualified success. I am not

Immigration-Mr. Woodsworth
so sure that the reason a good many more of them did not return to the old country was not simply that they had not the money with which to pay their passage. It may be all very well to get one harvest gathered by such a method, but I submit that a policy of this kind is not one on which we ought to depend to settle this country with the most desirable people.
With regard to foreign immigrants, I am not one of those who would advocate a wide open policy for immigrants from Europe; not because I have any prejudice against southeastern Europeans. I have a great many friends among them. I admire a great deal what they have accomplished in the old land. I have seen enough of their achievements in Canada to respect then}. But I say that we ourselves in Canada are not yet fitted to undertake the problems which the incoming of these immigrants introduces. We urge that we should get immigrants and then we are afraid to assume the responsibility which is entailed by their coming.
I should like to give a few figures by way of illustration from a report which I prepared some years ago for the governments of the three prairie provinces after making an intensive survey of over 1,000 Ukrainian homes in those provinces. I want to give some idea of the social and educational conditions which prevailed at that time in many of these communities and which still prevail to a lesser or greater degree. I noted that on the whole the immigrants remained isolated from their English-speaking neighbours, not so much because they wanted to remain isolated as because the English-speaking neighbours shunned the localities in which these immigrants were located. I also noted that the children were being gradually assimilated through the schools but in the process of assimilation they were losing much that should be retained. I do not think we can emphasize too strongly the necessity of urging these non-English-speaking immigrants to conserve the best things which they bring with them; too often we ask them to leave the old culture behind and forget that in so doing we are asking them to leave behind very much that is most worth while in the whole history of their nationality and in their own characters.
Again. I noted that the educational and social development is not proportionate to the material advancement. I could give you cases in which the Canadian-born children of these foreigners are not so well educated and not so well fitted to engage in the activities of citizenship as were the immigrants
themselves when they first arrived in this country. Let me speak particularly of the educational problem which we must face in a good many of our western communities, and in so doing I would like to give a few statistics. In the districts visited, which were fairly typical of those settlements all the way from Winnipeg to Edmonton, 68 per cent of the men did not speak English, 86 per cent did not read English and 48 per cent did not read or write at all. Of the 1,823 parents in the families studied 80 per cent did not speak English; of the other adults and children over fourteen years of age 53 per cent did not write or read English and 50 per cent did not read or write at all. Of the 1,253 children of school age 34 per cent did not attend school, 54 per cent did not read. or write English and 61 per cent did not read or write at all.

Compulsory education was not being enforced. I may say that these statistics were very carefully taken at that time; I had the name, the age and the residence of each child. In this connection iel me give a little illustration of the official attitude. I mentioned this condition of affairs to the then Minister of Education in one of the provinces-a province which rather boasted of the high standard of its educational attainments. He said, "Oh, well, that cannot be; we have compulsory education in this province." I said, "Well, I have the facts, and your province averages just about the same as the other two prairie provinces." Then that official said, "Oh, well, it would never do to let that become public; it would create a bad impression." I do not think any statement could better convey the attitude which we find all too often with regard to these matters. These facts must not be told the public for fear of creating a bad impression, yet at that time, although it was said that most of the children were attending schoo/

Immigration-Mr. Woodsworth
and there has been no subsequent census anything like so carefully taken of the districts visited in northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, 34 per cent of the children of these non-English-speaking communities were not given an opportunity to attend public school.

speechtext: May I ask a question? These statistics are for the year 1917; would the hon. member say they apply to-day?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I said they applied more or less to-day, but I am inclined to think that conditions have gradually improved. However, I would say that had I made that statement eleven years ago the officials would have said it was not correct, if there had not been the most absolute evidence to the contrary. I am not speaking of conditions just as they prevail to-day but I am speaking of problems with which we are still faced. These statistics are confessedly a little out of date, but they are the latest I have and they do give us some idea of this great problem.
Let me make it clear that I am not blaming the educational authorities of the three prairie provinces; they have done magnificent work in trying to meet this great additional problem which they have had to face. I do not think eastern members of parliament ever realized the problem which the immigrant has meant to the west. You have your English-speaking girls and boys whio do not need to learn to speak English; they may have to learn how to speak it more correctly, but they learn the language at home. In the west we have tens of thousands of children who have not that opportunity. More than that, we have had a good many people come to Canada in their young manhood and young womanhood who have had to pick up the language as be'st they could. In my own city of Winnipeg I suppose we have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on adult education simply because we felt it desirable that these people who come to us should acquire the English language as soon as possible.
That is the problem we have had in the west. I state the facts not to lay blame but to call attention to a situation. We have done the best we could, in building school houses away out in the northern districts, sometimes far from the railways, where it is almost impossible to attend school. In other ways we have done much, but I should like to emphasize the fact that this great task has been imposed upon us because of the immigration policy of this country. If we are going to import these immigrants we should

be prepared to see the job through and assume the responsibility created by their coming. Let me give one or two other points which I noted at that time, and again let me say that the conditions are somewhat improved by now, although in the northern districts I could find a good many similar communities to-day.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION

I too have lived among them. These statistics were secured for the governments of the three prairie provinces, and I want to bring before this house some of the problems that face us. Of the 937 families, 10 per cent lived in one room and 58 per cent in two rooms. I want to contrast that with some of the extravagant statements made in the Cardiff paper. Fifty-six per cent had no books, and 95 per cent no English books. Fifty per cent of the families did not take any newspaper, and 96 per cent did not take an English newspaper. In only about a dozen cases-all but three in Manitoba-was a doctor or a trained midwife

Immigration-M r. Woodsworth
present at the last birth. Sanitary arrangements were very primitive, and about two-thirds of the women, usually the younger women, worked in the fields. Practically all the children worked on the farm as soon as they were old enough. There was little provision or opportunity for recreation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
I am not trying to blame the foreigners. I have many friends among the foreigners and they know me, and they understand that. I am simply taking a select group which present more of a problem than the Canadians who have been here longer. If the hon. gentleman who has just spoken would like to get the economic side in favour of the foreigners, I will give it. It shows the wonderful progress made by these foreigners. Of the 832 families from whom information on this point was secured, 50 per cent started with no capital at all and 42 per cent with less than $500. Out of the whole number of families, 40 per cent had no debts at all, 40 per cent had less than $1,000 of debt, and 7 per cent over $5,000 each. In the great majority of cases they had secured a quarter, half or whole section, and in many cases the farms were in very good condition. I want to make it clear that I am not suggesting that these people are not good settlers; I should not like to give that idea to the house. They are among our very best settlers; they are people who have been accustomed to working on the land, and they are doing an excellent work. I do not want to suggest that they are in poorer condition than a great many Canadians in the outlying districts. Some of these Canadians are living under conditions similar to this. But the educational and social life of these foreigners present greater problems than the educational and social life of the Canadian people. The immigrants are not necessarily illiterate because they do not understand English. A great many coming here from northern Europe are well educated, some of them more highly educated than our own people, even although they do not speak English. 'Nevertheless, the ipresence of large groups of non-English speaking people in Canada presents a peculiar difficulty to us. A great many of those who came out at the time of the great immigration some twenty years ago, under the Sifton policy, were from southeastern Europe where at that time school education was not very common, and so a good many of them were illiterate when they came here. There is the other side of the picture. In our schools in Winnipeg to-day there is not a group that takes a higher standing than the children of these immigrants from southeastern Europe, and there are none that take higher standing in the university than those who come to us from various European countries.
Let me come back to the point I was trying to emphasize. There is no use in bringing in all these immigrants from the various countries of the world and then refusing to give special consideration to them or declining to accept the obligations put upon us. We will have to adopt- some policy of helping these people if we are to get the best from them. I should like to suggest a 'few recommendations which I have not the time to develop fully. The immigrants should be protected against exploitation, because they are particularly liable to this through their lack of knowledge of the English language. There should be provisions made for closer settlement than we have given them in the past. In some instance there should have been financial assistance and expert advice given, especially the latter, because many of tire immigrants have had to learn at great cost to themselves what they might have been told had there been am arrangement, such as we now have under the Soldier Settlement Board. There should have been a stricter enforcement of our school attendance, and curricula should be adapted to meet the needs of these newcomers. There should be special opportunities provided to enable the young people and adults to learn English. There should be instruction given in sanitation, and in farming methods, especially in dairying. This is being accomplished to a

Immigration-Mr. Woodsworth
greater degree to-day than it was at that time. There should be encouragement in the native handicrafts, some of which are wonderfully beautiful and would be a great asset if they could be developed. There should be a better mutual understanding, between Canadians and the immigrants. I wish I had the time to develop this point. We have brought these people in and to a certain extent they have remained foreigner's. We have maintained an isolated position. Unless this situation is altered we are laying up trodble for ourselves in the years to come.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: I have been trying to emphasize that if we are to benefit by the labour of the immigrant, we must not refuse to accept the responsibility which his coming creates. If British trade unionists, accustomed to the right of organizing, accustomed to social insurance, desire to have similar conditions in this country, we must not call them agitators. If we bring in people of other languages, we must not wonder that they want to have the language rights of the minorities of Europe. If we bring in people of alien habits and customs, we must not expect them to live like puritan Englishmen. The tirades which we make against the foreigners, calling them bolsheviks, merely reveal our own ignorance. The immigrant brings with him his own mental, moral, social, religious and political backgrounds. His backgrounds are not those of either English Ontario or French Quebec. It is for us older Canadians to find common ground with the newcomer. Only in this way can we prevent what might become something of a Balkanization of this country. Only in this way can we build up a greater Canada which will be not an English Canada or a French Canada but a larger and more inclusive Canada in the building of which all these various people will contribute.

I rise to dispel among other things two impressions which I consider are wrong impressions to go abroad from this house during this debate on immigration. The first is that we do not need immigrants and we should not encourage them. The second is that there are no opportunities for immigrants and that the government by its action has bludgeoned parts of our agricultural interests to such a

degree that they are not able to take advantage of the opportunities which I believe Canada possesses. As regards the first, this is a land of opportunity and we should encourage the right kind of immigrants. I do not believe we should humble ourselves in order to get them, but we should cause the people of other lands to realize that Canada is a land of opportunity and that as long as they are of the right calibre, we would like to have them. There are in this world two classes of people. The one bends to circumstances; the other compels circumstances to bend to themselves. The one is always beset with difficulties; the other clears those difficulties away. In the end the one becomes a living embodiment of what the qualities of energy, industry and perseverance shall surely accomplish, while the other exhibits the miserable wreck following indolence, indecision and want of purpose. It is the first class of immigrants that we wish to have in this country, and consistently with reason we cannot have too many of them.
The impression that we do not need immigrants and that we cannot make provision for them is, from my experience, contrary to the fact. From my experience, not only in my province of Ontario but after an extended trip last year over the western provinces, I believe, if we can get immigrants of the proper stamp, the men who, when they come to this country and realize, as is the truth, that we have great opportunities, will turn those opportunities to their own advantage, there is ample provision for them in Canada. We are looking for them on the farms throughout the whole of my province of Ontario.
The next is that we are not using the agriculturists of this country aright; that we are bludgeoning more particularly the dairy interests, and that under the present regime they have not a chance to operate. What do hon. gentlemen opposite want. That has already revealed itself very clearly. It revealed itself in the efforts which have been made across the floor to get us to pass other orders in council whereby we may repeat the action taken when the previous government came into existence for such a short time.
