speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not to speak of
butter but to deal with immigration. However, I greatly admired the indifference of the last speaker (Mr. McMillan) to all the joviality which interrupted his remarks. Just a few moments ago one of my friends asked how long I was going to speak, and I told him I would speak as long as the subject under discussion needed to be spoken to. I know there probably have been speeches which have taken up too much time, but I think hon. members will agree that I have never taken up the time of this house unnecessarily, and [DOT] I do not want to do so to-night. The other day in a book one of the hon. members on this side of the house lent me, entitled Disraeli, and which I have just handed back to him, I read of a little episode which happened in the British House of Commons. When Gladstone was a young man he asked his then leader whether in his speech he should be short and concise, but his leader told him to be long and diffuse. I will try to be as concise as possible, even though my speech may be a little longer than is necessary.
I was very much surprised when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) told this

house that he was an immigrant; I did not know that, and at the time I wondered if he came to Canada under any such scheme as the present proposed plan of decreased rates. I am sure if he had he would not have become the great man he is to-day; he never would have reached the eminent position he now occupies. Much has been said on the subject of immigration; many people would like to see this country populated over night; others would like to see immigration brought about gradually, and still others refute an immigration policy altogether from an economic standpoint. But no matter how we may view immigration the question is always before us pressing for a solution. Superfici-alfy we might come to the conclusion that Canada needs more people; we might say that Canada is such a vast country with such great resources that our population is absurdly out of proportion to our real and potential possibilities as a great nation.
Some people wonder why we should pay such a heavy toll for the upkeep of our roads, our schools, our transportation systems and other facilities which are necessary in this modern world. Every time I take the trip from Ottawa to Winnipeg or vice versa I am very much impressed by that uninhabited region through which I pass, and which adds to the burden we must carry to-day with regard to freight rates, and indirectly the up-keep of our great transcontinental railways, because of the few people who live in that region. In my opinion northern Ontario never will offer any inducement to immigration until something is found in that locality in the way of mineral deposits; until we find these minerals that region always will offer a serious obstacle to our economic development. Incidentally, I wonder whether something of this sort was not in the fertile mind of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) when he spoke of Canada being a geographical absurdity.
Of course it is in western Canada that the problem of immigration is now concentrated, because there we have some of the finest land in the world still unoccupied. Therefore the successful colonization of this land must engage the attention of the government if we are to derive any benefits from an immigration policy. Undoubtedly to-day the western farmers bear great financial burdens because of the sparse settlement of some parts of our country, and I have noticed that some members of this house have stated that these burdens could be greatly lessened if more of our land were occupied. They also say
Immigration-Mr. Luchkovich

that a greater settlement of the land would benefit not only the farmers but also the manufacturers; they claim that manufactures are not possible without a population, and that if we have no people in our country there will be no market for the products of our factories. They argue that manufacturers cannot exist unless there are markets, and since the consumption of goods must be local, the different localities must become populated. In other words we must have more people engaged in farming, fishing, stock raising and gardening.
So far as I have listened to the debate there seems to be no serious objection to immigration as such, but rather to the class of people we are bringing into Canada, the methods we are employing in order to induce them to come, and the inducements we offer to obtain the right type. As regards the proper class of immigrants that we should bring to Canada, I think the government, after thirty years of immigration, should know by this time the types which are most desirable for Canada. They should know the types that have become amenable to our laws and our constitution.
So far as the immigrants who have made new homes for themselves in Alberta are concerned, I can say most emphatically and without any fear of contradiction that they have become excellent home builders-not merely house builders but home builders. They have become home builders whose bodies and spirits are in Canada. There are some immigrants who come to Canada whose bodies are here but whose spirits are somewhere in New York, Massachusetts, Rhode Island or any of the other great industrial states of the American union. I have spoken of the word "home". I wonder if hon. members realize the full meaning of that word? On whether or not we realize the significance of the word home depends to a great measure the future welfare and well being of our country. If our immigrants have this home loving instinct I do not think	we	need	fear	forthe future of the country.	If	they	lack	it,I am positive in the belief that degeneration is inevitable. I contend that when a man comes to Canada with the main intention of building a home he has therein the fundamental qualities of good citizenship. If we are to have a policy of immigration, let us give the immigrant a chance to build for himself a home, and we can take it for granted that he will obey	our	laws	and	beamenable to our constitution.	I think	of
home as having a personal quality; it is
humanly and profoundly fundamental; it is made up of composite personalities, the people of one family who live in the same house and whose devotion to each other results in that elusive but much sought for thing we call happiness. When the German, Scandinavian or central European lands on our shores he first thinks of liberty, then a home, and then happiness. It is the same thing the loyalists had in their minds when they left the United States after the year 1776. When they come here do they become disillusioned? In some cases, yes, but in most cases, no. The immigrants who come here, especially from the northern parts of Europe, and even from the central parts of Europe, are too thrifty, too sturdy, too persevering and too determined to reclaim for themselves a home in Canada to be easily disillusioned.
As far as I have been able to observe, the type we have brought in here has been of the class which is poorest so far as material possessions are concerned. They lived very simply over in the old country; their food was the simplest and poorest, yet they throve very well on it. They had no home conveniences such as we have in Canada; their dwellings were the rudest, and yet they dearly loved them. Their family life was much deeper than is usually the case on the American continent, and their whole lives were circumscribed by their immediate surroundings. They lived in these little rude huts I have mentioned and their whole world was the land on which they lived. You may ask, Mr. Speaker, why it is the central European yearns so ardently for the shores of Canada. I think I have the answer; it is land hunger. It is that fervent desire to build for himself a home; it is that history making impulse that causes people to leave their homeland and seek foreign shores. It is the eternal march of humanity, the eternal search for happiness in ownership of the soil -in other words, a desire for a genuine home.
My feelings, Mr. Speaker, with respect to this subject are intense. If, therefore, any hon. member were to ask me what type I would want brought to Canada, I would immediately answer, the home loving type. It is home that makes character, and it is character that determines destiny, and it is home making that is. the mainspring of all civilization and human progress. All these elements are component elements; they are intermingled very closely and all spring from the one parent root-home. You might say, "Ah, but was it not the restless, cultured

Immigration-Mr. Luchkovich
and debonair Normans who conquered England in the year 1066?" My answer to that would be, Yes, but was it not the home loving Anglo-Saxon who finally assimilated the more cultured conqueror?
I think it would be a wrong policy, Mr. Speaker, to advocate the bringing over of large numbers of people in order to take away the jobs that rightly belong to the Canadian boys in Canada.

I met a man on the train the other day who wanted to know why so many of the immigrants who come to our shores are men with very little education. I think I can explain why. Most of them may be men without very much education, but they have very high ideals. I do not think our policy should be directed to bringing people into this country unless we are ready to give them work. I do not think we should embark on an immigration policy unless this country is ready for it from an economic standpoint. Furthermore, I do not think we should stimulate immigration by artificial means, because by doing so we shall only defeat the ends for which the immigration policy was inaugurated. By stimulating immigration artificially we discourage the pioneering individual and turn our immigrants into sissies or mollycoddles, whose only purpose in coming to Canada is to use this country as a back door through which to slip into the United States.

speechtext:
He is not a redblooded individual by any means. I have never yet known a man who appreciated a home that was virtually handed to him, and I have never yet known a man to appreciate a home which was not erected by the toil of his own hands or the sweat of his own brow. I have never yet known a home loving man whose home loving qualities were not engendered by honest, plodding toil.
I also think great care should be taken in the selection of our immigrants. The selection of our immigrants as well as the placing of them when they get here should be a government duty. The immigrants should be sound both in body and in mind, and they should be intelligent. They should be imbued with the idea that while the government is giving them a chance when they come here to build homes for themselves and therefore to share

in the benefits that such homes give them in Canada, they should at the same time be prepared to share with us the burdens and responsibilities that such citizenship entails. A learned man once said that "every choice we make is for an eternity," and it is only reasonable, therefore, to conclude that when the immigrant comes here, he and his offspring will remain in Canada for all generations and all time. Therefore if the government is to .continue its policy of inducing immigrants to come here it should bring in the type of immigrant that is adaptable to a country like ours. I may say, when I speak in this way, that I advocate bringing in people who are of peasant stock. The peasants are emphatically an adaptable type. A great poet once said:
111 fares the land, to hast'ning ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates and men decay;
Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade;
A breath can make them, as a breath has made:
But a bold peasantry, their country's pride,
When once destroyed, can never be supplied.
I do not think it is wise to embark upon a wholesale immigration to Canada. Just as I think it is folly to bring over to Canada the riffraff of Europe, so I think it is equally foolhardy to bring in too big an influx. Just as I think it is the height of wisdom to bring in the sturdy, pioneering, home-loving types, so I think it is equally wise that our policy should be one of quality rather than one of quantity. Premier Baldwin in a recent speech in Canada had this to say:
Canada has an enormous future and, if it be not impertinent to say so to Canadians, I would say: The future is with you; do not be in too much of a hurry. Your country is a country for virile races. Quality before quantity any day. Build up with the best. What does it matter if it is a hundred years or more before your country is full? Keep the stock you have, and the men and women you have, and see to it that the coming generations are in no whit inferior to them. I have often thought that it is a dangerous thing to the morale of a nation to get rich quickly, as it is to an individual. Time is on your side. Maintain the values; maintain the standards; and may the prayer of Canada always be the prayer of the Greek sailor, which has been preserved for us by Seneca: "God, you may save me if you will; you may sink me if you will; but whatever happens, I will always keep my rudder true".
There is a world of philosophy in that statement-"I will always keep my rudder true." Surely that is the spirit not of the mollycoddle but of the red-blooded pioneer.
Now that I have said something about the type of immigrant that we should allow to come into Canada, I shall speak for a few moments about the classification of those immigrants into the preferred, the non-preferred

Immigration-Mr. Luchkovich
and the undesirable. This classification in many cases is an unjust one, because those put on the non-preferred list might in some cases be placed on the preferred list, and it is possible that even some who are classed as undesirable might be put on the non-preferred or even on the preferred list. You cannot expunge a fact by a mere recital which is not a fact. I think it was Abraham Lincoln who once asked a friend of his this question:	"If
you call a dog's tail a leg, how many legs would that dog have?" The answer was: "Five." "No", said Lincoln, "You cannot make a leg out of a tail by merely calling it a leg." So in the same manner putting a man on the non-preferred list should not always mean that he is a non-preferred immigrant. I agree with what has been said about undesirable immigrants, that if they are not amenable to our laws and constitution, they should not be allowed to come into the country. I hope hon. members will not misunderstand me when I speak on the question of immigration. I make absolutely no differentiation as to race, or even religion. I speak merely on principle and I oppose the principle of extending financial aid to immigrants in order to stimulate immigration, because I think this is based on a principle that is fallacious, dangerous and absolutely inimical to the purpose for which it was inaugurated. Canada is still a young and primitive country. We have not yet reached the point where the modern conveniences of present-day civilized life begin and where pioneering ends. I have never yet heard in the history of the world of a successful subsidized immigration and I have also never heard of an overfed, pampered and petted person who ever amounted to anything. It is for that reason that I oppose any financial aid to immigration. I know it is dangerous to endeavour to teach a man to swim merely by throwing him into the ocean. But let us remember that there is always somebody in the crew who is ready to throw out a line in order to draw him back on to the deck of the ship. In the same manner in a pioneering community there is always somebody ready to extend a helping hand in times of greatest difficulties. Therefore, other things being equal, if the immigrant has the will and if he is made of the proper stuff, I have absolutely no doubt that he will make good in a country like Canada.
I have often wondered whether it would not be an improvement on our present system if something were done to make Canadian residents who bring in immigrants on affidavits actually responsible for those immigrants when they come into Canada. I have known cases where immigrants upon their arrival in Canada found that the people who had signed affidavits in order to bring them here repudiated the affidavits or eschewed all responsibility for them and would have nothing to do with the immigrants. I have in mind the case of a young girl who came to Canada about two years ago. She also came over here on an affidavit signed by an Alberta farmer. When she arrived, he eschewed all responsibility for his affidavit, and would not give her the work she expected to find when she came to Alberta. She is now being bandied about from one farmer to another, and they are taking advantage of that situation. She is receiving no wages, but is living in the hope that the work and the remuneration she expected to find in Alberta before her departure for Canada will be forthcoming. Cases like this are by no means rare. I merely cite this instance in order to give an example of what is being done, not only in the province of Alberta, but all over Canada. It might be argued, therefore, that only families already resident in Canada should be allowed to bring people in on affidavits. I personally think it would be a very good thing, because when the immigrant arrived in this country somebody in Canada would be responsible for him, and this would prevent the immigrant becoming a charge on the country and from joining the numerous breadlines which we have all over the country even at the present time.
With regard to the immigrants and their susceptibility to our .laws and constitution, and their readiness to accept those laws and that constitution, I know, that I am dealing with a subject that is of grave concern to many people in Canada. It is of grave concern for this reason, that they see in the coming of foreigners to our shores a potential menace to everything that they hold as dear as life itself.
I have noticed also that the coming of im- [DOT] migrants to our shores has caused a great stir in our social, political and educational circles, directed, no doubt, with a view to welcoming the immigrant and with a view to assimilating our immigration within as short a time as possible. The subject is at once a dangerous one, and also very contentious and very delicate. It is difficult indeed to deal with a subject like this without stepping on the toes of immigrants, and also without hurting the sensibilities of the native born. There are many realities in life such as religion, race, love and patriotism, which can be overdone. I intend to deal merely with the question of assimilation so far as it has to do with the questions of race and patriotism.
To begin with, there have been many plans for the quick assimilation of the immigiant.

Immigration-Mr. Luchkovich
One of them has been to sandwich the immigrant in with the rest of the races in Canada. So far as this sandwiching plan is concerned, I have this to say: I actually know how it works. It is possible to tolerate the immigrant only so far as he obeys our laws and also respects our constitution, but when it comes :o accepting him in our social circles, that is a different matter. It is a different matter also for the immigrant. What does it all result in? It results in the immigrant trying to seek his own level; in other words, he leaves the locality to which he originally came, and goes to another where he hopes to find his own level.
It has been said also that the segregation of the immigrants in large colonies is not conducive to ready assimilation, that it results in an imperium in imperio, or a nation within a nation. When we make remarks like that I think we stretch our imagination a little too far. The immigrant is a human being just like ourselves. He differs from us in no way except in language and certain racial characteristics, and surely in the matter of worldly-wise self consciousness he is not the sophisticated human being that a good many of ua are.
There have been two ways in which the immigrant has been looked upon in Canada. One is the mystical attitude, and the other is the rational one. The rational attitude is the one we employ in our everyday life. The mystical attitude is the attitude which we often adopt towards him when we are not in a very good mood, when we are not very well disposed towards him. The rational mood, I would say, would be the [more humane. The mystical attitude is the one which smacks more of prejudice, discrimination, and in less democratic countries than ours it virtually amounts to persecution. We on this side of the ocean are more sensitive than we appear. The mere vague annoyance which our own supersession in this country causes us is combined with our antipathy towards anyone and anything foreign. We are obsessed with that mystical attitude which repels everything we are not used to, and it is precisely this attitude which causes such a great gulf to be made between the different racial elements in our country. It is this attitude that makes us look with horror upon the farmer driving into town in his sheepskin coat, and upon the woman dressed in shawl and top boots coming home from market with a duck under one arm and a chicken under the other, in preparation for the family dinner. Why, even the foreigner's thrift and industry is viewed by us sometimes with hostility and suspicion. Of course we must recognize

that the Canadian views the foreigner from his own individual and very limited angle. He does not realize that the shadow of penury hangs very frequently over the newcomer and that everything he owns and attains in the way of the material things of life and education depends wholly upon his thrift and industry. The same can be said of the children of the immigrant at school. The immigrant's son or daughter must not fail, because he cannot afford to support his children on his paltry income. They must extend themselves to the limit at all times, for it is only by the greatest economy of finance that these poor people are able to get an education.
It is these things and a multitude of others that must be considered in the light of their effect upon the mind of the Canadian; for it is precisely these things that produce that typical mystical attitude towards the less fortunate newcomer. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I think if we were able to visualize ourselves in the immigrant's position we would realize exactly what his feelings are; we would understand his attitude better, and we would come to a more reasonable solution of the question than we have done up to the present. At any rate ft would help to break down the present barriers of misunderstanding between the different racial elements in our population, and it would also result in clear and sane thinking, without which no true progress can take place.
Now. sir, from what I have said with respect to this question I may be considered an ultra idealist, and my contribution may be thought impracticable, but I hope not. Despite everything that has been said against the immigrant, I think the day is not far distant when all the animosities engendered by racial conflicts not only in Europe but even on this continent will give way to a more reasonable attitude and will bring about a sound solution of the whole question. I look forward to the * time when all these racial misunderstandings will disappear and will recede into the dim and distant past as relics of a barbaric and savage age.

MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up a great deal of the time of the house, but I listened very carefully to the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) this afternoon. I do not know whether or not I misunderstood him, but I thought he said he went to the west twenty-five years ago. If that is the case I have been there five years longer, because I went there about thirty years ago. I think I went to that part of the country one year after my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) went to the west. My hon. friend chose to follow the 
practice of law, while I followed a different line of endeavour by taking up a brush homestead. I am not going to give personal experiences. but I want to point out, that there is a difference between immigration to-day and what it was in those days. When British Columbia came into confederation there was an agreement that a railroad should be built from the east to the west. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company built a colonization road, and I think my good friends the Liberals, if I remember aright-I came to Canada in 1878-said that the Canadian Pacific would not even pay for the axle grease. By going through that western country they opened up millions of acres of land on each side of the main line and the branches. There were millions of acres of free land, and interspersed with that were millions of acres of railroad land at S3 per acre. As soon as it became known that the land in the western country was fertile, immigrants poured in by the thousands. Why? Because the land was free. Just as soon as the homestead land began to be taken up, the $3 per acre land owned by the Canadian Pacific was in demand. In other words, we did unconsciously what our American friends had done; they put a railroad through the land first and the immigrants followed. Our policy more recently has been to let the immigrants get in by prairie schooners as well as they could, and the railroad would follow after they were in. What was the condition of the immigrants in 1898 when I was one? Just this: I had a free homestead and .all I had to do was to provide my living. The government bet me $10 I could not stick it out for three years; I took the bet and stuck it out for twenty. All I had to do was make a living and buy a couple of pairs of overalls a year in order to keep going. My hon. friend from West Calgary knows all about that. These settlers did the same thing, and when the $3 an acre land began to be taken up, it was a question whether it was cheaper for the immigrant to buy that land from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and work outside when he saw fit, or go on a homestead and be stuck there for six months in the year. At present there is no free land except away in the north country and the Peace River district, and there are no railways in that vicinity.
As far as the immigration policy is concerned, conditions have entirely changed. They are not the same as they were in the homestead days, and to meet the changed conditions you must adopt a different policy. If immigrants are brought in-I am not deal-

Immigration-Mr. Adshcad
ing so much with the question of how they are brought in, whether you pay their passage or not-the question is whether they can stick with it and make farming pay. As I have pointed' out, I had no obligations to pay on the homestead, I could just do as I liked as long as I managed to live. But the immigrant to-day has to pay $20, $25 or $30 per acre for raw land, and the problem is to make it pay after having to pay about $4,000 for a quarter section. At seven per cent interest this means $280 per year, and he has to live. At the present time I do not think he can do it. One thing that demonstrates this is the fact that we passed in this house last year what was called the revaluation act in respect to soldier settlement lands. Why? Because the soldiers had bought land at such prices that it was found they could not meet their obligations, and the land had to be revalued at lower figures. There are hundreds of farmers in Alberta and Saskatchewan-I do not know about Ontario-who bought land at these prices and under precisely the same conditions. They had no kind government to pass a revaluation act and take the burden off them.
Then during the war the farmers were told that the price of wheat would be set at $2.40 per bushel. That was not to keep the price up, but to keep it down. The farmer was the only person during the war time who underwent conscription of wealth. I remember seeing mounted police going through the district near Carbon, Alberta, and examining the wheat bins. They would say to a farmer, "You are keeping too much wheat. Of course you raise it, but we are only going to allow you to keep enough to sow your land, and we are going to take the rest at $2.40 per bushel." The farmer is the only person I know of who had his property, his wealth, conscripted during the war. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) hopes that we all will be in this position if there is another war. I know of farmers who bought land during the inflated war period, just as our soldiers bought it in 1919-20, and lost all because land values went down; they could not meet their payments and they were foreclosed. Where are the new settlers coming from? I do not care where they come from, whether Scandinavia or elsewhere, a large number of them are going on land held by speculators or corporations at from $20 to $30 per acre; that is where it is intended they are to go.
This question has to be dealt with on a business basis, just as a merchant will count his capital cost and his overhead and try to
meet interest and principal charges in order that his business may be a going concern. If he cannot do that he is bound to fail. The same thing is going to happen with the immigrant. If a farm can be bought under such business conditions that he can make it pay you will have no difficulty in bringing him in. Would there be any difficulty in the city of Ottawa if a man knew that a business that was a paying proposition was for sale and all he had to do was to go and take it? You would have a hundred applicants to-morrow. Just as soon as it is known that the farmer who buys land can make it pay, can pay the interest and the principal in proper proportion, and make a living and have something when he gets through, then you will have no difficulty in settling your lands and having a prosperous agricultural community. But that is what the immigrant cannot do to-day, and that is why so many are going on the land and then going off it.
My hon. friend from West Calgary was a solicitor for the gas company at one time, and in his very able manner he proceeded to present a case before the utilities commission. He took the affairs of the gas company before this commission and he charged their overhead, he charged the depreciation, he charged the interest on their plant and the cost of production and all that. When this was placed before the commission they granted a reasonable profit over and above 8 per cent on the invested capital. It does not really matter what the company got, b.ut they were allowed to charge 48 cents per thousand for gas. At that time oats were selling at Calgary at 25 cents a bushel. I happened to be in the council chamber at that particular time, and I went to my office and did some figuring. I took land at $25 an acre and I capitalized it. I knew what on the average a crop of oats would bring. I figured the cost of producing the oats, the overhead charges, the interest, the depreciation on machinery, and then I added just the same 8 per cent that the utilities commission added as a profit to my hon. friend's application in connection with the gas company. It worked out that those oats, to bring the very same profit which was allwed the capitalist, should sell at 60 cents a bushel, and the farmer at that time was getting 25 cents a bushel. I give that as an illustration to show that unless land is at such a price that a man can go on it as a business proposition in the same way as the hon. member for West Calgary figured in connection with the gas company, he cannot make it pay. If you reach that condition where he can make
Immigration-Mr. Adshead

it pay, you will have no difficulty in getting immigrants to take up farming in Canada.
There is another point that I want to bring out. I have seen some of the moving picture films which are taken abroad to show to prospective immigrants and I have also heard some of the speeches delivered to them and some of the conversations had with them in the old countiy. I do not know whether to make this as a charge, but I am sure I am speaking the truth. All the rosiest pictures of Canada are set forth. I have seen the pictures of "before" and "after". There is perhaps a plain praii'ie with a little log shack with a single room; then on the other hand there are the bumper crops, the cattle, the fine house, and so forth.	In other words what
they really do is paint just one side of the picture. It is only fair and right, if we are going to be honest with the prospective immigrants, that we should place both sides of the picture before them, because if they do not get it from us they will get it from some of their relatives on this side, or after they come here and go back home, they will tell their relatives at home their opinion of the country and the picture they will paint will be a very much exaggerated one. We know all about the frost, hailstorms, snowstorms, cold and other conditions we have in this country, and before an immigrant is induced to come out here, it is our bounden duty to give him both sides of the picture.
Various reasons have been presented why we should bring immigrants into Canada. I think one railroad magnate said:	We need
two million immigrants in the west; if we had two million immigrants here, our railway problems would be settled. That may be true from the railway standpoint and they are considering the question from that point of view. Another person said:	We should
have another two million people in the west; they would help to pay our national debt, and so forth. But the good of the settler and his future are not considered at all. What is considered is the benefit that would accrue to Canada and not the benefit that might accrue to the particular settler. We do not tell him, as we tell each other, that we want him here in order to relieve the railroads of the burden of over-capitalization, in order to help us to pay our national debt. We do not tell him those things. It is only right and honest that we should tell the settler the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, but in many cases that is not done.
That is the problem, and if you want to bring in immigrants, the farm lands which you have for sale must be offered at a reasonable price and in the far-off stretches where there

are no railways, colonization railways must be built, or else it must be made clear that when a man comes here with small capital the proposition will be a business one based on the same principle as that of my hon. friend in connection with the gas company.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
