speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend
to trespass at any length upon the time of the house in discussing this matter; but in view of what was said in the early days of the session when this committee was appointed, I think it is desirable to make a few general observations.
I cannot but think that the report of the committee will be very disappointing to many people in Canada. It certainly offers no new field for endeavour, nor does it offer any new suggestion with respect to the problems involved. I believe the Canadian people are firmly of the opinion that the problem is one of first magnitude calling for immediate action on the part of the government of the country. The reason I say that is greatly strengthened by what I observed from the government's statistics the other day with respect to the movement of our population. From 1897 to 1927, a period of thirty years, the population of Canada increased by 4,377,000. The population of Canada was 5,142,000 in June 1897, and in June 1927, thirty years later, it was
9.519.000.	or as I have said an increase of
4.377.000.	According to the same reports, between December 31, 1897, and December 31, 1927, we brought into this country 4,491,156 souls. That would mean that in those thirty years the country not only failed to keep the people it brought in but lost a part of its natural increase, because 114,156 more people were lost to the country than we brought in. That is rather a striking statement. According to the year book issued by the department the natural increase of population in those thirty years could not have been less than
2.600.000.	Therefore we have the astonishing result that in the thirty years from 1897 to 1927 Canada went, behind about 2,750,000 people. We brought in nearly 4,500,000; our natural increase was about 2,600,000, and yet our total net increase was only 4,377,000. Those are alarming figures; they are figures calculated to make every thoughtful Canadian pause-not pause and condemn governments, but pause and ask himself just why we have failed to keep in our country the population that we brought to it from other lands and also the young manhood and womanhood as it grew up in the country to man's and woman's estate. Those figures, as I read them from the report, made me pause, made me consider

Immigration-Mr. Bennett
again how serious is the problem with respect to immigration.
Canada moist have increased population if we are to maintain our position among the peoples of the world. We have provided facilities for a population of at least fifteen million people. We are carrying for the moment a debt of two and a half billions of dollars, necessitating annual interest payments, and a charge for pensions arising out of the great war, and for sinking fund, that amounts to a very, very vast sum indeed. The problem therefore is a pressing one. It is a problem that demands solution, and I have not yet concluded that the statesmanship of the Canadian people is not equal to the task that is imposed upon if. I believe that the vision and foresight of those who made possible this confederation have not been lost entirely to their descendants, and that we of this day and generation, if we but approach our problems 'as we should, in a spirit of goodwill, of unity of thought, of high purpose, of courage1, and of real ambition to serve our day and generation, may bring about their successful solution.
It is not in the narrow sense a party question. It is a question that far transcends party. It is a question that strikes at the very life and existence of Canada, and therefore I do think that those figures alone are sufficient reason why we should approach that problem not in any narrow sense, but as one of the first magnitude and of the greatest possible importance to this confederation.
With those very few observations, I turn to look for a moment at the result of this committee's efforts. I listened with much pleasure to the speech this morning and this afternoon of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). He endeavoured to support this report as being a sufficient justification for the efforts of the committee, and my friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) gave some reasons why he thought the results of the efforts of the committee should be viewed as being eminently successful. I regret that I cannot see in them anything that we should rejoice over, and I trust that I am not looking at the matter in any partisan, or narrow spirit. Where is there a ra.y of hope to those who will read that committee's report in the press of this country that any new policy will be inaugurated that will change the conditions under which we exist?
I do not propose to discuss the fiscal policy of this country or of the neighbouring republic. It is sufficient for my purpose to say that under a system of the highest protection the world has ever known, the United States
has attracted to its shores the largest population that has ever been brought into any country in the known history of the world and that population is to-day the largesl population living in one area, under one form of government, that we have in the world. They have their problems, problems of very great difficulty, but they were able to bring people into their country to such an extent that they now have a quota law against the free admission of the peoples of the world into the United States. That does mot in any sense indicate just what action, we should take here. I quite agree with my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior that that is so. But there are difficulties in connection with the solution of the problem in this country that were not known in the days when the United States were attracting people so readily to tihedr shores. This was referred to by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) and I cannot but think that the address to which we listened of that minister was by all odds the best speech he has made in this chamber. It was one that I think made all of us rejoice and feel a sense of pride that coming to these shores under the conditions he described, he has been able to make for himself such a place in this young Dominion. I am sure that he indicated in the very course of his observations one of the real powerful immigration agencies that should be at work in this country all the time, and that is the immigrant himself. Coming to this country as he did, a youth of seventeen., as a result of the inspiration that he received, he brought here eight people. That is t'he result. One satisfied immigrant brought here eight new settlers, and that is the way the population of the country grows. Unless we can create conditions that will bring about that feeling of satisfaction and pride in this country on the part of newcomers that governed and actuated my friend the Minister of Railways in inducing his father and sisters to oome to Canada to settle, we shall not be able to increase our population with that rapidity with which we should increase it. I feel quite satisfied that that is so.
But there have been many changes in the last twenty-five years. My friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Adshead) very properly referred to the changes that have taken place in all parts of Canada, particularly in that part in which we both reside. Distance has been annihilated; the attraction of the city has become greater than it ever was before; the building up of great industrial concerns in the great republic to the south has made it more difficult to attract new settlers

Immigration-Mr. Bennett

to our land; the difficulties in connection with a satisfactory return from the labour of the husbandman has also had something to do with it; but, on the other hand, there is no occupation that affords the same assurance of health and of enduring happiness as that which comes from toiling upon the soil and working the land. That, I think, is abundantly demonstrated by every man who has had any experience in that occupation, as well as by what we have been told by those who know the conditions far better than we do. But the attractions of the city are with us. The great war has also changed the attitude of mien towards occupations. The great war has changed the mental ouitlook of millions of people. On the other hand, it must not be forgotten that amongst the other nations of the world outside the British Empire, notably the German republic, you will find one of their most powerful journals referring to:
Europe's right to the use and development of these empty but fertile and healthy regions of the British Empire. "What right," is it asked, "has Great Britain to keep her Dominions empty?"
And the proposal is made that there should be some arrangement by which the League of Nations would take charge of settling the vacant spaces of the Dominion. That indicates a profound lack of knowledge of our institutions, an entire lack of understanding of what the position of Canada is within the British Empire, but, on the other hand, it indicates that there are people who are longing for the opportunity to settle the great open spaces of a country such as this. Now if the people of Germany feel that way with respect to it, and they have old age pensions and unemployment insurance, just as they have in Great Britain, we have a state of mind developed there that is somewhat different from the State of mind in Great Britain. Yet we know that there are congested conditions in Great Britain. We know that there is there a surplus population that desires the opportunity for advancement, the opportunity to gratify their ambitions, to make new homes for themselves, to own and possess land, and after all, the same idea that was in the mind of the young immigrant of twenty-seven years ago, the love of adventure, the love of the soil, the desire to own a home, to live under the flag of his fathers, is still in, the minds of large numbers of young men and young women in Great Britain. But they do not come here, because, rightly or wrongly, they have in Great Britain the idea at the moment that we do not want them. I charge against this administration that during the last few years

there has grown up in Great Britain the idea that the people of Great Britain are not wanted in Canada. I read it in their morning papers, in the Post and in the Times; I read it in their evening papers; I read it in their weekly magazines. They have that idea firmly entrenched in their .minds, and it has come about not wholly without some reasons, because of difficulties that have been experienced, for instance, in connection with medical examinations, difficulties experienced when they came here, the idea that they are dumped down on the land and left there, difficulties in finding work-these and allied matters have made many of the people of Great Britain believe that they are not wanted in this country. The idea has been, of course, fostered to some extent by countries which require settlers just as much as we do, but the idea I mention has got abroad and it is painfully apparent to those who have visited England in, the last ten years, since the war at least. The idea is firmly embedded in their minds that we do not desire those settlers in Canada. That idea is, of course, erroneous, but it has been fostered by conditions to which I have alluded. Under those circumstances and under those conditions, there was brought into being last year a new plan of medical inspection, notwithstanding the fact that according to the reports issued by our o,wn department there were very small numbers of rejections of those who had been examined in England. I am happy to say that one of the recommendations of the committee, insisted upon by the medical men on the committee, will change this and may have very far-reaching and beneficial results. But that in itself was one more factor that made the people think we were desirous of excluding them from this country, although rejections at ports of entry on medical grounds of immigrants from the British Isles were comparatively few. In 1920 they amounted to 21; in 1921, 99; in 1922, 60; in 1923, 37; in 1924, 130; in 1925, 83, and in 1926 only 40. Those are the figures according to our own returns. Nevertheless this new medical plan put in force last fall had very disastrous results, for a friend of mine, a former Canadian, who is vitally interested in the settlement of this country by British people, sent me word as soon as the committee began its sittings that as long as those medical regulations were continued it was no use making any attempt to get British settlers into this country. Then unfortunate occurrences, such as that to which my hon. friend from Halifax recently directed attention, have also done something

Immigration-Mr. Bennett
to neutralize our efforts towards getting new settlers. These are the real conditions that confront us.
But what have we on the other side? We have a great country with a small population. We have millions of acres of untouched land within twenty miles of the railway; we have great fisheries; we have lakes and rivers; we have vast mineral deposits-we have gold and silver and nickel; we have extensive forests. In a word1, we have everything that goes to make a great people; that is, we have a great estate. What are we doing to develop this estate? That is the question. The question of immigration is tied up with the question of colonization. Colonization, of course, means work. That single word is the key to the whole situation-work.	Work
must be provided not only for our own people but for newcomers. I have said so often- I repeat it now-if you go to the old communities of this country you find men and women are leaving, not because they wish to, but because there is no work for them to do. Yet we have the greatest estate that any people ever had committed to their hands in trust to develop. But we are not developing it. True, we are taking away some of the minerals, we are taking something from the forests, we are getting vast wealth from the soil with the limited number of people employed. And I want to place myself upon record that it is a fallacy to believe that the bringing of more people into Canada means the cheapening of labour and the lowering of the high standard of living of those who are here. History teaches us that if you get people settled in a 'country you are making work. Every time you bring a new productive person into the country, whether he be productive by his hands or his brains, if you are unifying your efforts, you are always opening up new avenues of work. That has been the history of other countries, and I am sure it will be the history of this country.
Now, with this vast estate and with our limited population, we have brought in, as I say, a large number of immigrants, but we have not kept them here, we have not even maintained our natural increase. What is the obvious remedy? Not what the committee's report indicates, but the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), namely, that we should have a great department-a department of immigration, colonization and industry, divided into two branches, the one dealing with the securing of immigrants, coordinating its efforts with the provinces, and the other see-
56103-248J
ing to it that there is work for those people when they come here, and not only for them but for those who are already here.
I do not propose to-night to enter into a discussion of the policies necessary to achieve the second result. There may be acute differences of opinion between us with respect to that, but this I do say, that every possible legislative power of this parliament, together with the powers of the provincial legislatures, should be exercised to carry into effect the idea contained in the creation of the second branch of that great department. It was suggested by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that these two things are not related one to the other. Why, they march hand in hand; without the two it is impossible to succeed. I will take an illustration that came under my own observation and with which I at least in my youth had something to do. East of Calgary the Canadian Pacific Railway Company induced the government of the day to permit them to take the balance of their grant lands in a solid block containing an area of about three million acres. It was surveyed by competent surveyors.^ They said: An irrigation system is essential if these lands are to be made productive. An analysis of the soil showed that these were fertile lands if properly watered. For this purpose the waters of the Bow river were available. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company spent millions of dollars on an irrigation canal in the western section and the central section, and they spent further millions of dollars in developing these lands and making them fit for the settler. They then spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in the endeavour to get settlers, and I am bound to say that in the first instance their expectations were disappointed; they got no such results as they expected. But they did not stop. They went forward then and developed the eastern section at a further vast expenditure. They found difficulty in getting settlers to come in of their own volition, so they divided the country into ready-made farms, provided with suitable buildings, stock and implements. To-day when you pass through that country as I did only last week you see comfortable homes, well-kept barns and well-tilled land, with evidences everywhere of the amazing prosperity that comes to those who till migrated land under conditions such as exist there. As I surveyed the scene it gave me a sense of pride that we have in our country an institution that was willing to risk its capital to the extent I have stated to bring about those results.
Immigration-Mr. Bennett

I regret to have to differ with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways as to relying entirely upon unorganized and individual effort as we used to do twenty-five years ago. But conditions have profoundly changed in the meantime. They have so profoundly changed that, as mentioned this afternoon, there is a very great demand for settlers made upon Britain and upon various countries of northern Europe from which we draw population, with the result that we are not able to secure all we wish from those countries. Australia and New Zealand are in the same plight. But, on the other hand, we can get our fair share if we make conditions here such as are found in other communities, and therefore it is necessary to give that assistance to immigrants which otherwise we would not be compelled to give. So we must take example by that private enterprise to which I have referred. There may be failure, seeming disaster, but with perseverance and determination we must go forward with the work, regardless of the prospects, until at last success crowns our efforts. That is vyhat we must do with this estate.
This is only magnifying by thousands the irrigation work of the Canadian Pacific. This is the same problem as they had to face, only there is added to it something more. The Canadian Pacific found very early that mere agricultural development was not sufficient; they realized that you must add to that some industrial activities. So they endeavoured to get a beet sugar factory, and there is now a small establishment at Raymond in southern Alberta. True, it is not in the irrigation block to which I first referred. It is in the old Galt irrigation block southeast of Lethbridge. There you have an idea of the beet sugar industry. I did not realize just what one industry means in the life and development of a country until I analyzed it on the ground in connection with that sugar beet industry. It was an amazing revelation. I followed its processes from the time the beets were put into the ground until the sugar was put into the bags. There was SI ,000,000 of an investment in that factory. I found that a number of men were engaged in making the soil ready for the beets; a number of others planted the beets in the soil; others, again, were engaged in connection with the management of waters and canals and the caring for the plants during the summer, constantly freeing them from weeds. Then I began to see them being taken up, put into cars and by cars transported to the factory. That, I found, reacted

so that the repair work on these cars was reflected in the shops at Calgary. I found miners busily engaged getting out the necessary limestone for transportation to the factory for the purpose of clarifying the beet juice so that it might be made into sugar. I found coal men employed, a number of men mining some 10,000 tons of coal for the purpose of running the factory. That one industry, with all its ramifications, from the work in the fields, the planting of the beets, up to the time the sugar was placed upon the market, gave employment to a vast number of men-indeed, an amazing number compared to what one would expect. Men were engaged, as I say, in activities of various kinds: planting beets, gathering beets, weeding beets; there were train men, engineers, firemen, conductors; there were coal men, repair men, limestone men. And finally there were those who sold the finished product over the counter.
That single industry, developed as it was in southern Alberta, furnishes an illustration of the point I desire to make with respect to the second branch of the great department which should be set up in this country, in relation to the industrial side of Canadian life, to give employment to settlers. The minister will tell you that there is no more prosperous settlement in western Canada than that settlement in southern Alberta which utilizes these sugar beets and operates that factory. There you have work and settlement, settlement and work, the one coordinated with the other. There would be no work if there were no settlement, nor would there be any settlement if there were no work. And this factory has brought back to Canada men who had left it. The same conditions existing there have made possible settlement in parts of the United States whence those settlers came.
Let us take another illustration: take the development of our mining industry at Trail, for example. That is an illustration of the development which can take Iplace in an industry from very small beginnings. Because of an economic survey made, because of the determination that there was something there worth trying to get and worth maintaining, the effort which was exerted there has succeeded. Take other branches of activity. Take linseed oil, if you will; from the flax you have the linseed oil. The same may be said with respect to flour.
In 1915 the late Sir William Van Home was asked to be chairman of an economic commission in this country having for its purpose the very idea which is now set forth

Immigration-Mr. Bennett
in this amendment-the idea of determining by survey what the possibilities of this country are as regards industrial development and the utilization of our vast resources, and side by side with that the settlement of new people. Settlement and work; settlement and development; settlement and employment: these things must go side by side in any policy worthy of the name.
Now I regret to say this-you will say it is very unkind of me to say it. But the fact is that we have not at this time, in charge of this department, a gentleman who by natural aptitude or training is calculated to properly develop policies in connection with the Immigration department. I have as profound a respect as any man in this house for my hon. friend the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). But in England they have long since, in their parliament, made it a rule under conditions such as these to fearlessly express their opinions with respect to ministers of the crown who direct policies. And in this instance I regret to say that it is painfully apparent to anyone, whoever he may be, whether Liberal or Conservative, whether he sits to the right or to the left of the Speaker, that the hon. gentleman, the member for Brandon, a man of integrity and character, is unfitted temperamentally or by training to discharge the varied and onerous duties of Minister of Immigration and Colonization in this country. That is one of the real difficulties. You could not have made the Canadian Pacific irrigation projects flourish unless you had had at the head of them a man such as the late Lord Shaughnessy or men of that type. And so, in relation to our immigration policy, you cannot have that policy succeed if you put in charge of it one who is disqualified-not qualified at least- either by training or by temperament, to discharge the very onerous duties that appertain to that position. So we say in this amendment that we should have a responsible minister in charge, although in Australia they did try a commission. And there are those in this country who believe that a commission responsible indirectly to the government might be able to succeed. In Canada there is less evidence of the likelihood of a commission succeeding. We say there should be a strong minister, a minister with the training, with the aptitude, with the temperament, with the desire and the determination and vigour to make such a department succeed- with these two great branches working side by side, the one, in cooperation with the provinces and other organizations, seeking new settlers, the other providing work for these
settlers when they come here to keep them in this country. For I deny that this country is, by reason of its natural resources, unfitted for occupation, unfitted to give employment to men who come within its borders.
This criticism we make strikes at the very foundation of existing conditions. You will never make this department succeed, it cannot succeed, so long as it is presided over by the gentleman who now controls it, surrounded by those who sit with him. It cannot be done; it will not be done. And therefore we venture to offer that criticism. We offer it frankly because we believe it is in the public interest .that it should be made, with no desire in the world to hurt anyone's feelings. However fit and proper, however able the hon. gentleman may be to discharge duties in other places, he is wholly unfitted for the discharge of duties in the portfolio which he now fills.
A step further. My hon. friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) this afternoon, in a very humorous and at times pathetic speech, dealt with the kind of settlers we are bringing in. I venture to say to him that he overlooked one point. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) dealt with it in part, but he did not in my judgment deal with it whoLly. The reason we are seeking British settlers is not ' that we attach so much more importance to them as settlers than to any others, but that our institutions are moulded and formed, and have been for generations, upon British models. And we believe, we are firm in the conviction-as I believe the government is-that the only way in which we can maintain these institutions is by continuing to bring to this country a proper modicum of settlers who understand and appreciate them. That is the real reason.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext: Are not the laws of the United States moulded on British institutions, and have not their people come from every part of the world in tens of millions, conforming to British institutions when they arrive in that country?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cartier has entirely misapprehended the point. Read the history of the United States, read what is written in every magazine in that country by thoughtful men, and you will find that the principle of the melting pot has failed; and they are quite apprehensive. Every thoughtful man in the United States, every keen observer, every man who travels, every author, everyone who shapes and moulds public opinion in the universities and in the great foundations-all these are bewail-
Immigration-Mr. Bennett

ing the fact that uncontrolled immigration has been permitted into that country, to such an extent that there is now in the United States a polyglot papulation, without any distinctive civilization, and one about which many of them are in great despair. That is the answer to my hon. friend. And, sir, it is because We desire to profit by the very lessons we learned there that we are endeavouring to maintain our civilization at that high standard which has made the British civilization the test by which all other civilized nations in modern times are measured.
_ I quite agree with what my friend the Minister of Railways and Canals said this afternoon. We are bringing people into this country from all the countries which were mentioned by my hon. friend, but the report does not add to or take away from the countries; it merely names those countries from which the people have come. I have in mind at the moment Germans whom I know well, who came to this country many years ago. Some of them went weal, about the time I went there; some came later and some had been there earlier. I look upon their splendid homes and I realize that they are making a very great contribution to the life of our country. The older settlers-mark you, I say the older settlers-all law-abiding citizens, we appealed to them through their own great national heroes. Now we are endeavouring to make the appeal through the heroes of our own country, those great fathers of confederation who laid the foundations of this Dominion. The celebrations which took place in Canada last year commemorating the sixtieth anniversary of confederation were intended to carry out that very idea and to give effect to that very purpose. At least that may be said with safety. I have in mind families of Ukrainians; one hon. member who spoke to-night, although bom in the United States, is a descendant in the second generation of a central European people. I have in mind their homes; I recall the circumstances under which many of them came to settle in this country. They came from Austria and from other states some of which are ^ now a part of Russia. I saw their first beginnings; I saw their sod huts, and years later I saw their beautiful homes, surrounded by trees, with all the comforts which go to make life happy. These people adapted themselves to our conditions, and they have made excellent settlers. We have Germans and Ukrainians; we have people from other countries, Norwegians, Swedes, Danes, Finns, Germans, some Swiss, some Dutch, some Belgians, a few old country French, some

Austrians; I recall a very considerable settlement of people from that country. We have people from Poland, a few from Roumania; I have never seen any from Bithuania, but that was part of another country before the war, and the same might be said with respect to Edthonia and Latvia. I have seen some few settlers from Czechoslovakia and Jugoslavia, which countries were parts of Serbia before the war. These people have made excellent settlers; they have kept the law; they have prospered and they are proud of Canada, but if cannot be that we must draw upon them to shape our civilization. We must still maintain that measure of British civilization which will enable us to assimilate these people to British institutions, rather than assimilate our civilization to theirs. That is the point; that is all that may be said with respect to it, and it is the point I desire to make at this time. We earnestly and sincerely believe that the civilization which we call the British civilization is the standard Iby which we must measure our own civilization; we desire to assimilate those whom we bring to this country to that civilization, that standard of living, that regard for morality and law and the institutions of the country and to the ordered and regulated development of this country. That is what we desire, rather than by the introduction of vast and overwhelming numbers of people from other countries to assimilate the British immigrants and the few Canadians who are left to some other civilization. That is what we are endeavouring to do, and that is the reasoh so much stress is laid upon the British settler, not upon the Englishman as the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophaii) said, but upon the British settler as indicating that standard of civilization on which we build our institutions and to which we hope to be able to make those who come to us not conform but assimilate, so that they may play the part in it that we ourselves play, that they may realize that the same conditions exist as in days gone by, when the people said "wherever the king's writ ran, there was freedom and liberty of conscience." So everyone who lives under British institutions in that part of 'the Empire which we call Canada may have freedom and liberty, regard for law and order and a desire for an ordered government of which they and we may well be proud. That I say to my hon. friend is our reason, rather than the reason which he suggested this afternoon.
As far as I can see it is the purpose of all governments to maintain that position; that is the intention of all governments, but we

Immigration-Mr. Ralston
do say that there has been a singular lack of appreciation of that position during recent years by the present government. In various sections of western Canada they have planted colonies from far-off lands, who have settled upon the soil and maintained their own peculiar civilization rather than become assimilated to that British civilization which should prevail in this country, 'because there has not been a sufficient leavening of it to ensure that result. That is one of the complaints we make.
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken longer than was my intention when I rose, but I cannot too strongly urge upon this house the real gravity and seriousness of the problem with which we have to deal. My hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) referred to the length of his residence in western Canada. I have also lived there for a great number of years, indeed for the major portion of my life since I attained manhood, and I have seen it grow and prosper. I have seen the difficulties which have been experienced and I have seen great problems solved by private enterprise. I have seen great communities settled; I saw the Calgary Colonization Company settle a great area near Calgary; I saw the valley of the Saskatchewan settled by private enterprise. Surely what can be accomplished in that regard by private enterprise can be accomplished by the government. I saw a great railway carry out the enterprise to which I have already referred. This country, east, west, north and south, from Cape Breton to Vancouver Island, is but a vast estate, and as I have so often said it is an estate which we hold in trukt to settle and develop. What a reflection it is upon us that to-day there are less people, less tenants on that estate than the number we have brought in during the past thirty years together with the natural increase. What a reflection that isl But there is yet time to remedy the difficulty; there is yet time to solve these problems, and that can be done only by the creation of a body charged with responsibility and presided over by men of vision, of hope, of courage and of determination, who will look upon obstacles not as factors to deter them from going forward with their work but rather as difficulties to be overcome, to spur them on to greater effort. But, Mr. Speaker, these men do not sit upon the treasury benches of this country; such men are not directing this work and are not putting their minds, their hearts, their strength and their courage into this matter as they should. Because they are
not doing so and because we believe that the enunciation of proper policies, the placing upon the statute books of proper legislation and the creation of proper departments of the government would bring about these results, we have offered this amendment with its constructive suggestions for the good of the country, rather than the piecemeal report of the committee which means nothing. The report of the committee is a mere statement of platitudes except for the last paragraph, which was included because it was thought it might temper the minds of some of the hon. members who sit on this side of the house to the extent that there would be unanimous adoption of the report of the committee. But that report in itself is not ample or sufficient, because it does not strike at the foundation of the difficulty, which is failure not only to bring people into Canada but to keep them here and to provide them with work.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN REPORT OP COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
At this late hour I do not intend to detain the house at any length, but in view of the fact that I happened to be a member of that committee I do feel that the attention of the house should be directed to one or two matters which have been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I think the house will bear me out when I say that my hon. friend has not offered anything new in the way of a solution for the immigration question. He has contented himself with stating that this is a great problem, which everybody knew. He has contented himself with stating that the population of Canada has not increased as fast as we would desire. He has also stated that employment is a very necessary corollary to immigration, and I think almost everybody knew that. I do not think there is anything very constructive in the speech of my hon. friend, except the suggestion that there should be the words "industrial development" added to the name of the Department of Immigration and Colonization. I do not think the country will regard that as a very constructive contribution to this debate or to the immigration problem.
Regarding British immigration, no one deplores more than the members on this side of the house what my hon. friend has suggested-I am not prepared to say that it is a fact-that British people have the idea that they are not wanted in this country. If any proof were needed of the fact that they are wanted, I think that proof will be found when our friends in the British Isles read the first portion of this report, which sets out the
Immigration-Mr. Ralston

attractions which are offered in order to induce British settlers to come to this country. I am not going to detain the house at any length in referring to them, but when we remember that all British subjects, no matter what their occupation may be, are welcomed to Canada and are eagerly sought after to come here; that special efforts are made to bring them here, it will be seen that we do welcome them. In addition to that, agricultural labourers have been given a reduction of 90 per cent in the passage rate they are required to pay to come to this country; British domestic workers are given a like reduction; the families of agricultural labourers are being brought out on that same 90 per cent reduction; British children over 14 and under 17 years of age brought here by voluntary societies have their passage paid free of charge by the Canadian and British governments; provision is made for the training and placement of British boys in farm homes, and a special grant is made to societies who bring them out, this grant being more than the amount of the passage. The federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments and the British government, have arranged a special tripartite agreement, which has already been entered into by two provinces and a third is negotiating in regard to it, whereby the British government supplies 81,509 for stock and equipment, the Canadian government recruits the settler and supervises the settlement, and the provincial government furnishes the farm. In addition to that the Canadian government shares on a fifty-fifty basis in any loss in connection with the loan and shares any loss of interest on the price of the farm. There is also the three thousand family scheme, which is just about completed, in connection with which the Canadian government furnishes the farm on easy terms, the British government furnishes a $1,500 loan for stock and equipment, and the Canadian government provides additional assistance by way of selection, settlement and supervision free of charge. There is also the land settlement scheme for British boys, under which the Canadian government contributes $1,000, the provincial government $250, and the British government $1,250. When these things are really considered the people of the old land will realize that we do want British settlers here.
When I say further that this government spends $16.67 per head for administration expenses and in connection with the assisted passage scheme for British settlers as compared with 11 cents per head for immigrants from other countries, it seems to me it is a
(Mr. Ralston.]
pretty practical illustration of the desire which Canada has to have Britishers come to this country. I do feel that it is mistake to give utterance to this idea, or give any credence to the statement that British settlers are not wanted.
Reference has been made to the matter of medical inspection. This house knows and the committee considered it in its report, that this medical inspection was put in mainly for the purpose of assisting the British emigrant and seeing that there is no chance of his coming to a port of embarkation and arriving on this side and being turned back because the Canadian doctors do not pass him. The Canadian government has at its own expense placed Canadian doctors on the other side to provide for examinations at some 350 centres in order that the British emigrant might have the examination made over there and know at the outset whether or not he would be accepted in this country. That was the purpose of the medical examination. That examination was not put into force in any capricious manner. Representations were made by the steamship companies, by the provincial governments, by the Dominion Council of Health and by other social service organizations, who all agreed that this would be a good system to put into effect. I submit that the system has not been given a fair trial.
Influences, to which I will not refer tonight, have started a certain amount of publicity and propaganda in the old land. Perhaps there have been those who fear their interests may by adversely affected in some way or other by this system of medical examination, and they have started propaganda with the result that some British people got the idea that this was a restrictive measure. The committee felt, not because they had not faith in the system of medical examinations and not because they considered it had been given a fair trial, that these examinations had better be conducted by local British doctors under the supervision and control of the Canadian organization. The committee was endeavouring to convey to the British people that it was not the desire of the Canadian government to let them have even an idea that there was any intention of restriction in this regard. As my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said, that has been recommended by the committee, and I feel that the publication of what I have already referred to will set at rest the fears of our British brothers with regard to our desire to have them over here.

Immigration-Mr. Ralston
My hon. friend has referred to the matter of the great migration to the United States. We all know there has been a very large increase in the population there, but I want to say to him that I think it is to the credit and pride of Canada that we, situated side by side with that great nation which is supposed to offer the greatest attractions to immigrants of any country in the world, have been able to maintain our population as we have. We have been capable of increasing our immigration during the last three years from that very country to our own. In 1924 we had 11,000 coming from that country. This has been steadily increasing; in 1926, 21.000 came and in 1927, 25,000, the last group having something like $14,000,000 of capital and assets. I think it is to the credit of Canada, and I think it dispels some of the gloom which my hon. friend has tried to shed over this chamber and which his speech may spread over this country, when we remember that people from the United States, that supposedly attractive country, are coming here in these large numbers. In this connection let me read an editorial from an independent paper, the Daily Record of Sherbrooke.
Unless it is the unanimous desire of the house to continue, I would call attention to the fact that it is now eleven o'clock.

I was going to read this
editorial from the Daily Record of Sherbrooke:
Trekking Northward
They are coming here. Great vans, loaded with household goods, are on the move from New England mill towns northward to Quebec. It is easier to make a living here than there. So many Canadian families are returning.
A few years ago the movement was all in the other direction. Many who went did not better themselves. They received high pay for their work. But the job was not steady. In a few months they realized that they would have been better off had they remained in Canada.
This north or south movement is inseparable from economic conditions. Quebec province and Canada in general are prosperous. There is a greater proportion of unemployment in the states than here. Hence the reversal of the migrant movement.
Let me deal for just a moment with what my hon. friend has suggested with regard to the matter of work. I am afraid he has not read the report very carefully.

If he had and if he had studied what has been done in the way of immigration and of providing settlement and employment, he would remember, as I have suggested before, that in the matter of settlement of those from the old land, agricultural settlers particularly, special assistance, to which I have already referred, has been given by the Canadian government. But those are not the only immigrants who are coming here. In addition to them there are immigrants from continental countries. In respect to them, as my hon. friend should recall, we have an agreement with the railways and that agreement recognizes the principle which my hon. friend has laid down, namely, that there shall be settlement; that employment shall be provided, because it is specifically stated in the agreement that the railways shall provide settlement for the people they bring in. This is no new principle; this is not the first time that it has been enunciated. It has been long recognized as part of the policy of coordination of the colonization principle with the work of immigration.
I want to point out to my hon. friend the second thing which he has overlooked. If he will read the report over carefully, he will find a declaration of what I regard as a somewhat new principle, a recognition of what may be a more effective settlement agency than even a federal department, and that is this, that settlement and employment conditions perhaps can be more intimately and closely looked after and supervised by the provincial administrations. There is in the report a paragraph which points a way to that and which suggests a remedy which I think my hon. friend should take note of. He had in mind
Immigration-Mr. Ralston

the necessity for providing settlement and the best way to do it. The paragraph which is found on page 6 is as follows:
The committee recommends that special efforts be now made to extend the field of activity of the provincial authorities particularly in the matter of placement, settlement and supervision of immigrants, and that, with this in view, the federal government consider contributing to defray the cost of provincial cooperation for that purpose.
The idea is to be taken along with what is set out in the preceding paragraph, as follows:	.
_ In the opinion of the committee the responsibility and control of the selection of immigrants, no matter by whom recruited must rest solely and exclusively with the government of Canada.
But after the immigrants are selected, after the arrangements are made for their transportation, the matter of placement, settlement and supervision is regarded as being one in which the provincial governments can very effectively cooperate in seeing to it that the work to which my hon. friend has referred is provided. It is no mere gesture, because the committee has suggested that a contribution to the cost of provincial cooperation in that respect be made by the federal government.

I can only say to my hon. friend that he was a member of the committee which unanimously concurred in the report and I do not think I ought to be asked to interpret it for him. I think the report means exactly wha't it says, namely, that the field of activity of the provincial authorities particularly in the matter of placement, settlement and supervision of immigrants, can be extended and that the federal government should consider contributing to defray the cost of provincial cooperation for that purpose. That takes care of exactly the idea to which my hon. friend has referred, but it does not do so through some sort of distant department of industrial development set up by the federal authorities in Ottawa. It provides for cooperation by the people who, as I said a moment ago, are perhaps in a more close and intimate position to look after the matter of placement, settlement and supervision of immigrants. That is a forward step; that is a matter that has not formerly been stressed as strongly as we might hope for in connection with the colonization and immigration of this country. I believe along those lines rather than along the line suggested by my hon.

friend, namely, by adding the words "industrial development" to the Department of Immigration and Colonization, is the way to see that those who come to this country are properly settled.
I want to say wh'at my hon. friend has also omitted to note, namely that this report, states that although we are to do what we can in the matter of immigration, placement and settlement of those who come to us from other shores, we are not to forget the boys, girls, young men and young women of Canada and we must endeavour to see that they are given a fair chance as well.
May I refer just for a moment to the amendment which my hon. friend has moved. It recommends a department. The department is already established. It proposes to add to the title the two words "industrial development." It mentions 'a superintendent but I suppose there is nothing much in the name and the duties would really be those of a deputy minister and that title would do just as well. Let me refer to the duties which this department is supposed to perform. There is the co-ordination of all organizations in connection with the matter of immigration. That has been the policy of the Department of Immigration and Colonization ever since it was established. It has been coordinating and working with all these various organizations. It has assisted them in connection with their work. In connection with the inquiry which has just been held the committee have had many representations from them regarding their work with the department. It is also suggested that they will see that the immigrants are physically and mentally fit. We do not need to have any new department for that. Provision is made in the act for that and the matter of medical examination is for that very purpose. The suggestion is made that financial provision be made for settlement. If my hon. friend will look at the report which has been concurred in unanimously, he will find that in the matter of land settlement the committee has made a pretty definite recommendation.

speechtext:
The committee had heard the evidence with regard to the three thousand

Immigration-Mr. Ralston
family settlement scheme and they felt that opportunity should be given to see how that scheme would work out. A very large commitment had been made by the country in connection with that scheme. They had in mind the soldier settlement scheme in which the country had invested many millions of dollars. They had in mind also, although it is not mentioned in the report, the fact that provision bad been made for farm loans; that the farm loan board would assist not only those who came to this country but those who are already here, and the committee recommends to parliament that time be given to see how this scheme works out before embarking on extended schemes of that .character. I think from what I have heard around the chamber to-day there is a great deal of unanimity in regard to this particular .part of the report which suggests that the farm settlement scheme should be allowed to pass the experimental stage and that we have the benefit of the experience in regard to it before we make further large financial commitments. That is what the committee has to say in regard to the question of financial assistance in the matter of settlement.
As regards the reference in the amendment to settlement in the new provinces of those from the older provinces, I only want to say that I happen to come from one of the older provinces and I feel equal opportunity should be given for settlement in the older provinces of those who may have gone to the newer provinces and who would like to come back.
The next suggestion is that the department should direct schemes of settlement. If there are no direct schemes to be put into effect, there are no functions in that respect for the department to carry on. But the department already has ample machinery for that purpose in the land settlement board, which has been operating for a good while.
In the second part of the amendment there are really only two points. One is that there should be an economic survey of this country taken with a view to ascertaining the opportunities for employment. As has already-been pointed out, this report expressly recognizes that idea and the very last paragraph contains a most comprehensive statement of that policy in words which have been already read, but which I shall take the time of the house to read again:
Your committee would also recommend that the government make an intensive and comprehensive study of the possibilities of increasing industrial and agricultural development in
Canada with a view to attracting capital and providing wider and increased opportunities for employment not only for our own people, but for prospective immigrants.
The suggestion in the amendment is also that the industrial development branch shall advise as to future economic development. I want to remind the house that we have already a branch of natural resources in the Department of the Interior. We have already a Department of Trade and Commerce, which makes an intensive study of this kind of thing. We have a Bureau of Statistics which I think some gentlemen on the other side of the house referred to the other night as being in every way efficient, and with these agencies at our command it seems to me that we ought to be in a fairly good position to be advised as to our future economic development without setting up any more machinery for that purpose.
There is also the suggestion that attention should be given to the establishment of suitable industries in small towns. I do say that after the economic survey has been made it seems to me it may be time enough for this government to consider cooperation with the provinces in that respect, but so far it has been the practice that the establishment of industries is a matter of provincial jurisdiction and provincial scope, and I think it would be laying down a somewhat dangerous policy to suggest that this federal government shall now embark on the scheme of establishing industries in various small towns throughout the Dominion.
With those remarks I think I have dealt briefly with the teeth of the amendment which is before the house. I do fail to find, with all due respect to my good friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) whose work as has already been stated, has been on such a high level in connection with the whole deliberations of the committee, I do fail to find in his resolution anything new or anything which will provide necessary machinery which we have not already.
My last word is that it seems to me that this report points to a redoubling of effort, to a uniting of resources, to a uniting of all the activities which will go to make the work of immigration successful-not to leave out the provincial authorities, not to leave out the voluntary organizations, not to leave out all those agencies which can help to bring into this country a desirable population, and w-hen that population comes here, see to it that it is properly settled and properly placed. I feel that the report of the committee

Immigration-Mr. Mackenzie King
will perhaps be found to have more of hope and more of new ideas, and to contain a great deal more in the way of constructive policies for the future than anything which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has indicated in the rather doleful speech which he has delivered to-night.

Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to take any part in the present debate, especially in view of all that has been said, and I would not now do so had it not been for some remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) this evening. For some reason best known to himself, my hon. friend has found it advisable to go outside of the report which we have been discussing to reflect upon a very loyal, a very faithful and a very able colleague, the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) in his administration of the department. I feel that I should be belying every instinct which I possess if I permitted a reflection of the kind, particularly with my knowledge of the minister's qualifications for the position which he holds, to pass unnoticed, and to pass without a very severe censure, if it is permissible for such words to pass from my lips.
The hon. leader of the opposition reflected on my colleague by referring to him as one who did not possess the necessary training or temperament for the position which he holds. That, I think, was the gravamen of his indictment. I would say to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that he is the last person whp ought to speak of temperament. I shall not say anything about his training. I think probably it was a matter of temperament which for the moment caused him to make the remark which he did make.
May I say this, and I say it in all sincerity to my hon. friend: I belive that in commenting as he did upon the Minister of Immigration and Colonization he was giving expression to what he believed was expected of him as the leader of the opposition in voicing a certain critical attitude, rather than giving utterance to his own personal convictions. My hon. friend was careful to say that in British public life men speak fearlessly with respect to those who are opposed to them in parliament. I am sure that in commenting as he did my hon. friend was giving expression to what he believed some members of his following throughout, the country would wish to hear voiced. But may I ask with respect to the criticism, on what grounds is it based? Why

does my hon. friend say that the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization is not suited by training and temperament to fill the position which he holds?
What has been the training of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization? I ask hon. members to consider the training which the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization has had as fitting him for the portfolio which he holds, and to compare it with the training of other ministers who have held that position, or compare it with any training which a man could possibly have who was going to be called upon to fill the position of Minister of Immigration.
The minister came to this country as a young man; he came to Canada as an immigrant. As an immigrant he went to western Canada, was educated in part in this country, took an active interest in the municipal life of the community in which he lived, was appointed a reeve of the municipality in which be was residing, subsequently was made secretary-treasurer of the union of municipalities, clearly indicative of the fact that his fellow men believed that he was one who had a wise and a wide knowledge of the needs of those who were similarly situated to himself. He brought up his family in a new community, himself as a settler, himself one who was making a home in the new land, and he did it so successfully and so completely that he won the confidence of his fellow citizens in the district in which he resided to such a degree that on three separate occasions they have returned him as a member to this parliament of Canada.
May I add that when there grew up in this country, as there did immediately after the war, a party which was inclined to feel that the two old political parties did not represent to the extent which they thought it should be represented the feeling of the great agricultural interests in this country, and when that party became sufficiently strong to be recognized as a separate party in this house, its representatives in parliament chose the present Minister of Immigration as the leader of their party, and as their leader he held an honoured position in this house.
I cannot but believe that the feeling of hon. gentlemen opposite, if they share the view expressed by their leader, is due to the circumstance that the present Minister of Immigration sits to-day on this side of the house instead of on the opposite side, rather than to any feeling that is entertained towards the minister himself. I say, Mr. Speaker, I can

Immigration-Mr. Mackenzie King
think of no career better calculated to be of service to one in the position of Minister of Immigration and Colonization than a career such as I have described, and no example to others more inspiring. Take those who are thinking of emigrating from the old country to this Dominion. Many references have been made to the fact that we are not obtaining the number of immigrants from the British Isles which we should all like to see coming to this country. I ask you, what greater inducement could be offered to any young man about to seek a home in a new land, whait finer example than that which is to be found in the career of the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization? He is a living example of what this country offers to men who possess his sterling qualities. They can find in this land great opportunities, and there is no position to which they cannot hope to rise provided they possess the qualities which my hon. friend possesses in such large measure.
In the course of this debate with respect to immigration, we have not stressed sufficiently the exceptional position which many of those who have come from the British Isles as immigrants have attained in our Dominion. I am proud to be able to say that in the present administration at least three distinguished members-the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) who spoke this afternoon, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) who is being referred to to-night, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) who at the present moment is representing Canada, at Geneva-came' to this country as emigrants from the British Isles, one from England, one from Scotland and one from Ireland. Could there be a better advertisement of what this country offers in the way of opportunity to British settlers? If it be necessary to mention another example, I might recall the memorable gathering which took(plaee only a year or two ago, when members of this house who originally had come to Canada as emigrants from other countries gathered together, to the number, if I recollect aright, of twenty-seven, to celebrate that particular circumstance. Knowledge of that kind spread throughout the world is to my mind the best sort of immigration propaganda this country has to offer. If we are not getting a larger number of immigrants it is due in large measure to the fact that too little stress is laid on, these outstanding successes, while too much is said by hon. gentlemen opposite in bemoaning conditions in this country.
May I say this further word with respect to the temperament, so-called, of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization? What, may I ask, is required in the way of temperament on the part of a minister of the crown to enable him adequately to fill a position which has to do very largely, in fact almost entirely, with human relations and human life? The first quality I should say is broad human sympathy, the second, a great desire to be of service to one's fellow men.
I venture to say that hon. members, irrespective of party, will agree with me that no member of this house possesses those two qualities to a finer or in a larger degree than does the present Minister of Immigration and Colonization. Indeed, if he has been willing to take upon himself the heavy obligations of that department it is, I believe, primarily because he has as a life purpose the desire, which I believe is one held in considerable measure by all who are in public life, of being of some real service to his fellow men. But I would say this further with regard to my hon. friend: I believe he honestly feels that the greatest service which it would be possible for him to render to this land1 and to his fellow men is to bring an opportunity similar to that which he himself has enjoyed, within the range of as large a number of his fellow men as may be possible. I know that the great desire of the minister while he is holding his present portfolio is to be the instrument of helping others to share opportunities such as he as a young man shared, and to enjoy the privileges which he and his family have enjoyed in our Dominion. These are qualities which, as I have said, all hon. members recognize in the Minister of Immigration.
But may I add that if the minister needed any testimony to his successful administration of the department, he has it in the report of the committee which has been presented to-day. In days when it was possible to give to settlers free homesteads, to advertise free homesteads; in days when it was possible for men and women to bring their families from the old land to the new for a few dollars instead of having to pay the relatively enormous rates which are charged to-day by the steamship and railway companies, it was an easy matter to fill this country with immigrants. There were a large number of people, seeking to emigrate from the British isles, who were anxious to get away and it was then an easy matter to bring them in. But what are the facts today? Every single dominion has been competing for immigrants from the British isles; and so far as this Dominion is concerned1 Canada under the administration of the present minister has had the largest number of immigrants from the British isles. Moreover, while hon. gentlemen opposite in the last few years have been complaining about the numbers of Canadians leaving Canada for the United States, under the present minister Canadians have been returning in larger numbers than ever before.
I say, therefore, without wishing to prolong the discussion, that whether one is to judge the administration of the department by the actual records as they speak for themselves under the administration of the present minister; whether one is to judge by the temperament which should be possessed by anyone whose duty it is to deal with large numbers of human beings seeking to make homes in a new land under conditions which, to most men, must be unknown unless they have been matters of experience; or whether it be the matter of training, my hon. friend and colleague, one of the most loyal, devoted, industrious and efficient of ministers of the crown, no matter by which of these qualifications he is to be judged, will be found to hold an honoured position in this country.

speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that a message has been received from the Senate acquainting this house:
1.	That the Senate doth insist on its first and second amendments, striking out the letter (a) in line 1 of clause 2, and paragraph (a) of clause 2, because by reason of a subsequent amendment to clause 25 herein set out, clause 2 (a) serves no useful purpose.
2.	That the Senate doth insist on its sixth amendment, striking out clause 7, because under section 11 of the Pension Act all who served in a theatre of war have been pensioned or are pensionable to the full extent of their disabilities without any deduction in respect of their pre-enlistment condition. The existing law clearly provides that even those who were found by medical examination to be unfit for front line service shall also be pensioned to the full extent of their disabilities notwithstanding the fact that their service in a theatre of war was of a non-combatant character, far removed from the scene of active hostilities. The existing law which has been in operation some ten years is definite and is well understood. Clause 7 proposes an amendment thereto providing that pensions shall be awarded to dependents where the aggravation of a preenlistment injury or disease substantially contributed to death. Consequently this is obviously intended to cover only those who served in Canada and England. The difficulty of interpreting the words "substantially contributed", coupled with the fact that the present law seems to be sufficiently generous to cover all classes that would come under this clause, warrant the conclusion that it cannot be reasonably justified.
3.	That the Senate doth amend its seventh amendment by substituting for new section 21

(X) of clause 12 the following:
"21. (1) Nothwithstanding any of the provisions of this Act, any case respecting a member of the forces or any of his dependents which is claimed to be specially meritorious and in which pension has been refused by the Commission, or if an appeal lies to the Board, both by the Commission and by the Board, may be made the subject of an investigation and adjudication by way of compassionate pension or allowance as hereinafter provided."
4.	That the Senate doth not insist on its ninth amendment, striking out clause 25, but substitutes the following new clause 25 in lieu thereof:

'32. (1) No pension shall be paid to the widow of a pensioner unless she was living with him or was maintained by him or was, in the opinion of the Commission, entitled to be maintained by him at the time of his death and for a reasonable time previously thereto.
(i)	No pension shall be paid to the widow of a member of the forces unless she was married to him before the appearance of the injury or disease which resulted in his death,
(a)	Unless the injury in respect of which he was pensioned or entitled to pension would not shorten his expectancy of life; or
(b)	Unless he was not chronically ill of a pensionable disease and not in receipt of pension in respect thereof.

That the Senate doth insist on its twelfth amendment, amending clause 31, because under the existing law the soldier himself, or in the event of his death his widow, his children or his parents have the right of appeal on the ground that the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death was attributable to or wras incurred during military service. Paragraphs (a) and (b) of this clause, while not clear, are intended to change the existing principle of the right of appeal, particularly for dependents other than widows and children who claim their financial resources are inadequate.
